ECET – 231

Lab - 1

Orientation – Safety and Lab Familiarization

Introduction:

The Hampden console is an integral unit containing both AC and DC power supplies and metering equipment. This appendix describes the equipment and the meter settings. The left side of the console contains AC power supplies and AC metering. The right side contains the DC power supplies and DC metering. The bridge between them contains two AC wattmeters.

The layout:

The AC side: At the top is a group of three meters. The center one is a voltmeter and the two meters on the outside are ammeters. The power supplies are located on the pedestal. The top circuit breaker is the main circuit breaker for the entire console. When the main breaker is off there is no power to any of the console. The top breaker operates the duplex receptacle just to the right of the breaker and the three phase 208/120 Volt jacks just below the breaker. The lower breaker operates the variable three phase 0 to 240/140 Volt jacks just below the breaker.

The DC side: At the top is a group of four meters. The in the center are two ammeters and the two on the outside are voltmeters. The power supplies are located on the pedestal. Both of the circuit breakers are dual switches. The top circuit breaker operates the variable 0 to 150 Volt jacks just below the breaker. The lower circuit breaker operates the variable 0 to 125 Volt jacks just below the breaker.

ECET – 231
Electrical Power and Machinery Laboratory

AC Equipment on the Console

AC Power supplies:

Three sources of AC power are available on the left pedestal.

Fixed 120V, single phase, 3 wire, 10A duplex receptacle.
Fixed 208/120V, three phase, 4 wire 6A
Variable 0 to 240/140V, three phase, 4 wire 6A

Turning on the main breaker turns on the duplex receptacle, the fixed 208/120V, and an indicator pilot light.

Turning on the lower breaker turns on the variable voltage supply. Adjusting the voltage control knob adjusts the line to line voltage from 0 to 240V and the line to neutral from 0 to 140V on all three phases.

The circuit breakers will trip in the event of an overload. Remove the cause of the overload before resetting the circuit breaker.

AC Meters

There are two AC ammeters and one AC voltmeter. The meters are diode protected against overloads as high as 1000%. Hampden claims 3% accuracy for the voltmeter and 2% accuracy for the ammeter.

Lab 1   2 of 12

Page 5 of 39 · Source photo: 20261104_092318.jpg (Google Drive fileId [redacted-id]).

ECET – 231
Electrical Power and Machinery Laboratory

AC ammeters:

The console contains two AC ammeters with four ranges: 0 to 0.5, 0 to 2, 0 to 4, and 0 to 8 Amps.

Connect the ammeter, in series, so all the load is passing through the meter. Set the meter to the off position before applying power to the circuit.

The meter has only two scales on the faceplate, 0 to 0.5 and 0 to 2. To obtain the actual current on the two higher ranges it will necessary to multiply the meter readings.

On the 0.5 or the 2 Amp settings, read the current from their respective scales.
On the 4 Amp setting, read the current from the 2 Amp scale and multiply by two.
On the 8 Amp setting, read the current from the 2 Amp scale and multiply by four.

AC voltmeters:

The console contains one voltmeter that has two ranges: 0 to 150 or 0 to 300 Volt.

Connect the voltmeter in parallel with the voltage to be measured. Set the toggle switch to off position before applying power to the circuit. If the voltage is less than 150 volts set the toggle switch to the 150V scale. The voltmeter has dual scale of 150 and 300 volts, read the voltage from their respective scales.

AC/DC wattmeter:

There are two multi-range wattmeters between the pedestals. To prevent damage to the wattmeter always set them to the off position before applying power to the circuit.

Connect the current coil in series with the load current and the voltage coil in parallel with the load voltage. The left terminals of the two coils (looking at the console) should be connected together. Turning the switch to the straight up position turns the meter off. Turning the selector switch CCW (counter clockwise) sets the potential coil to 150V and the ampere coil to the value selected. Turning the selector switch CW (clockwise) set the potential coil to 300V.

There is only one scale on the meter face. The meter reads directly only on the 150V/2A setting. For any other setting a multiplying factor must be used. These multiplying factors are shown under the selector switches on the console.

Choosing the 150V potential coil and an 8A current coil has a multiplying factor of 4.
Choosing the 300V potential coil and an 8A current coil has a multiplying factor of 8.

DC equipment on the Console

DC Power supplies:

Two sources of DC power are located on the right pedestal. Each is protected with dual circuit breakers.

Variable 0 to 150V 1A

To activate either DC power supply the main breaker must be on. The upper set of circuit breakers operates the variable (small knob) 0 to 150V power supply. This supply should be primarily used to power the field circuits in the DC motors. Both breakers must be on to complete the circuit.

Variable 0 to 125V 5A

The lower set of circuit breakers operates the variable (large knob) 0 to 125V power supply. This supply should be primarily used to power the main winding. Both breakers must be on to complete the circuit. Either of the circuit breakers may trip in the event of an overload.

DC Meters:

The DC ammeter and the DC voltmeter are diode protected against overload. Hampden claims an accuracy of 2%.

Lab 1   4 of 12

Page 7 of 39 · Source photo: 20261104_092329.jpg (Google Drive fileId [redacted-id]).

ECET – 231
Electrical Power and Machinery Laboratory

DC ammeter:

The ammeter must be connected in series with the current to be measured. The (+) terminal must be connected to the most positive side of the circuit. The (-) terminal must be connected to the most negative side.

There are four current ranges on the ammeters: 0 to 0.5, 0 to 1, 0 to 2.5, and 0 to 5 Amps. The 0.5 Amp switch selection is read directly on the 0 to 0.5 Amp scale. When the 5 Amp position is selected read the 0 to 0.5 Amp scale as if there was no decimal in front of the 5. When the 1 Amp position is selected double the reading on the 0 to 0.5 scale. The 2.5 Amp switch selection is read directly on the 0 to 2.5 scale.

Note: If the needles move downscale below zero, turn off the power and reverse the terminal connections on the ammeter.

DC voltmeters:

The voltmeters are connected in parallel with the voltage to be measured. The (+) terminal connected to the positive side of the circuit and the (-) terminal on the negative side of the circuit.

There are two ranges on the voltmeters: 0 to 75 Volts and 0 to 150 Volts. Both are read from their respective sides of the scale.

Equipment with the Console:

DM – 100A DC Machine:

The DM – 100A is a two-pole, compound machine consisting of a shunt field, series field, and an armature winding. A shunt field rheostat, line fuse, and a two-pole starter switch are also included part of the control box.

ECET – 231
Electrical Power and Machinery Laboratory

Operation (DC motor)

The proper connections to operate as a compound DC motor as shown in figure 1. With the proper connections made the motor can be started by moving the motor start switch toggle up (on). It is a good practice to set the shunt field rheostat to its minimum resistance, fully counter-clockwise (CCW). Minimum resistance will allow the maximum starting torque and the minimum starting current. The desired motor speed may be adjusted by adjusting the field rheostat or varying the line voltage.

Operation (DC generator)

The proper connections to operate as a compound DC generator as shown in figure 2. With the proper connections made, drive the generator at approximately 1800 RPM with a suitable motor. It is a good practice to set the shunt field rheostat to its maximum resistance, fully clockwise (CW). Rotate the rheostat CCW until the desired output voltage has been reached. The output voltage can be sent to the resistance load by moving the generator start switch toggle up (on).

SPM – 100A AC Split Phase Motor

The SPM – 100A is a single – phase, four – pole machine consisting of a dual wound stator and a squirrel – cage rotor. A two – pole circuit breaker, main winding, and start winding with centrifugal switch are included in the control box.

The following are the ratings for the AC motor.

Winding Type:Dual Wound Stator
Rotor:Squirrel Cage Rotor
Horsepower:⅓ HP
Speed:1725 RPM
Voltage:115 Volts 1φ
Current4 Amps
Frequency:60 Hz
Insulation:Class B
Maximum Ambient Temp:40° C
Rating:Continuous
Starter
Type of Operation:Toggle
Number of Poles:Two
Overload Type:Thermal
Trip Rating:8 Amps
Reset MethodPush Toggle Down

Operation (AC motor)

The proper connections to operate as a compound DC motor as shown in figure 1. With the proper connections made the motor can be started by moving the motor start switch toggle up (on). The split phase motor is started by having two separate windings wound in the stator. One winding is used only for starting and it is wound with a smaller wire size having higher electrical resistance than the main windings. A centrifugal switch is used to disconnect the starting winding when the motor reaches approximately 75% of rated speed. The motor then continues to run on the main windings.

ECET – 231
Electrical Power and Machinery Laboratory

RL – 100A Resistance Load

The RL – 100A is a variable resistance unit used to apply a resistive load to generators or alternators. One unit may be used in a single phase application or a bank of three units may be combined for three phase applications. The RL – 100A introduces resistive load in 16 steps, designed to produce approximately equal increments of load current. The internal resistors are connected in parallel and are rated at 100 watts each. The SPST toggle switches are numbered and must be closed in numerical order to maintain a balanced load.

PB – 100 Prony Break

The PB – 100 is a measurable mechanical load device with an inch – ounce spring scale, 6” diameter pulley, belt, lever arm, adjusting knob, and counter balance weight.

The following are the ratings for the Prony Break:

Full Scale Torque432 Inch - Ounces
Maximum Speed3000 RPM
Scale72 Ounces / 2000 Grams
RotationEither Direction
AdjustmentsKnob Variable from Zero to Maximum Load
CoolingConvection
RatingIntermediate

Operation (PB – 100)

With the motor coupled to the Prony Break, the shaft and pulley will rotate at the same speed as the motor. Turning the adjustable knob clockwise will tighten the belt against the pulley. The drag caused by the friction of the belt produces a load on the motor. The lever arm is free to pivot below the adjustable knob. The drag on the belt is directly counteracted by the spring scale (maximum 72 ounces). The scale is located 6” from the pivot (which is the same as 2 * radius of the pulley). Multiplying the spring scale by 6” will give the value of the load in inch – ounces, using the formula Torque (T) = 2 * radius (r) * force (F) T=2rF. If the scale does not zero then subtract the starting amount from the actual reading to get the force.

The Prony Break can be used in either direction rotation. The spring scale must be mounted on the front or the rear so it acts in tension for the direction of rotation. The counter balance weight must be hung on the opposite end of the lever arm from the spring scale.

Ametek 1723 Tachometer

While not part of the Hampden equipment, each of the consoles has a tachometer in the cabinet. The tachometer draws power from the duplex receptacle. Console Familiarization and AC Power Measurement

Objective:

  1. Familiarize you with the Hampden power console and AC metering equipment.
  2. Learn the proper connections for a resistive load to the AC source and measure the voltage, current, and power.
  3. Learn the proper connection, start, and operate an AC single-phase motor. Make the same voltage, current, and power measurements as the previous step.

Equipment:

  1. Variable AC Volt Power Source (0-140 use “A” and “N” on Panel HMD – 100 – PPC – AC)
  2. Fixed AC Volt Power Source (120 use “A” and “N” on Panel HMD – 100 – PPC – AC)
  3. RL - 100A Resistance Load
  4. SPM - 100 Single-phase Induction Motor
  5. AC Wattmeter
  6. AC Voltmeter
  7. AC Ammeter

Procedure:

  1. Make the connections shown in Figure 1. Each member of the lab group should verify that the circuit is connected properly. Have the Instructor (and/or the Lab Assistant) check the circuit.
  2. Always set the Voltmeter(s) to the highest value before turning on the main switch. Also, turn the Ammeter(s) and Wattmeter(s) to the OFF position until the actual readings are to be read.
  3. Set the resistive load to 100 Ohms.

Note: On the RL-100A Resistance Load the internal resistors are connected in parallel and are rated at 100 watts each.

Saturation Curve of a DC Generator

Objective:

To determine the relationship between the no – load (open circuit) voltage and the shunt field current of a (separately – excited) shunt generator.

Equipment:

  1. 120 Volt Single – phase Power Source (use “A” and “N” on Panel HMD – 100 – PPC – AC)
  2. SPM – 100 Single – phase Induction Motor
  3. Variable DC Power Source (0 – 125 Volts on Panel HMD – 100 – PPC – DC)
  4. DM – 100A DC Machine
  5. (2) DC Voltmeter
  6. DC Ammeter

Procedure:

  1. Make the connections shown in Figure 1. Each member of the lab group should verify that the circuit is connected properly. Have the Instructor (and/or the Lab Assistant) check the circuit.
  1. Set the Voltmeter(s) to the highest setting. Set the Ammeter(s) to the OFF position.
  2. Turn on the main AC power on panel HMD – 100 – PPC – AC.
  3. Turn on the Primary and Secondary switches on the DC power (0 – 125 VDC) on panel HMD – 100 – PPC – DC. Start the AC motor by turning on the motor start switch.
  4. Set the shunt field voltage to 120 VDC. Start the DC generator by turning on the generator start switch.
  5. Adjust the generator field rheostat to cause a current of 0.35 amps to flow in the shunt field with 120V across the field circuit.

  1. Vary the voltage applied to the generator shunt field, from maximum to zero, zero to maximum, and back to zero. Observe voltage output on the generator.

  1. With zero shunt field current, measure the armature output voltage and record in Table 1. Measure and record the output voltage for six additional increasing values of the field current. (DO NOT EXCEED the rated field current.)

  1. Now measure the armature voltage for seven decreasing values of field current and record in Table 1. Follow the note as indicated after problem 7, in reverse order.

REMINDER: To maintain the proper data for the saturation curve, the shunt field voltage should not be increased until zero is reached. If the next value is passed slightly (do not increase), record the output voltage at that value.

Lab - 4

Load Characteristics of a Self-Excited Shunt Generator

Objective:

At rated speed and voltage:

  1. Obtain the load characteristics of a self-excited shunt generator.
  2. Determine the internal (generated) characteristics.

Equipment:

  1. Variable DC Power Source (0 – 150 Volts on Panel HMD – 100 – PPC – DC)
  2. Variable DC Power Source (0 – 125 Volts on Panel HMD – 100 – PPC – DC)
  3. (2) DM – 100A DC Machine
  4. Resistance Load Unit RL – 100A
  5. Photo LCD Tachometer
  6. (2) DC Voltmeter
  7. (2) DC Ammeter
  8. Digital Multi-Meter (DC Volts)

Procedure:

  1. Make the connections shown in Figure 1. Each member of the lab group should verify that the circuit is connected properly. Have the Instructor (and/or the Lab Assistant) check the circuit.
  2. Adjust the motor’s field rheostat to its minimum resistance, fully counter-clockwise position.
  3. Adjust the generator’s field rheostat to its maximum resistance, fully clockwise position.
Lab 4   1 of 3

Procedure: - cont’d

  1. Set the Voltmeter(s) to the highest setting. Set the Ammeter(s) to the OFF position.
  2. Turn on the main AC power on panel HMD – 100 – PPC – AC. Turn on the Primary and Secondary switches on both the DC power sources (0 – 150 VDC and 0 – 125 VDC) on panel HMD – 100 – PPC – DC.
  3. Set the shunt field voltage and the motor voltage at exactly 120 volts.
  4. Start the motor. Using the tachometer set the motor speed to 1800 RPM. Adjust the speed by varying its field rheostat as needed while maintaining the motor armature voltage at 120 VDC.
  5. When the motor speed is at 1800 RPM, adjust the generator’s output to 140 volts DC by adjusting its field rheostat.

REMINDER: Keep the motor speed at 1800 RPM by adjusting its field rheostat and/or motor voltage.

  1. Turn on the generator start switch. This will allow the Resistance Load Unit to simulate a load on the generator.
  2. Perform a load test on the generator from no load to the full load by turning on the switches on the Resistance Load Unit.

Note: When one load switch is turned on it is considered to be one load step.

  1. With the switches all off on the Resistance Load Unit record the generator’s armature voltage (VA), load current (IL), field current (IF), and speed (RPM) in Table 1.

REMINDER: Turn on the switches 1 thru 16 consecutively. Then turn them off 16 down to 1. If a switch is turned on or off out of order the circuit will be broken.

Note: As each load step is added it may be necessary to adjust the field rheostat and/or the motor voltage to maintain the motor speed of 1800 RPM.

  1. Continue recording the data, in Table 1, after each load step until all 16 switches have been turned on.
  2. Shut off the generator start switch and the motor start switch. Shut off both power supplies. Disconnect all the connections before measuring the generator armature resistance.
  3. Use the DMM to measure the generator armature resistance and record the value above Table 1.

Note: To get the correct resistance rotate the shaft slowly and record the minimum value.

  1. Calculate the generator’s armature current (IA) and armature voltage drop (VD) due to the armature resistance. Record these values in Table 1.
  2. Calculate the generator’s internal generated voltage (VG) and record the value in Table 1.

Note: If the power factor of the circuit is less than 50% one of the pointers will reverse (go below zero). Turn off the motor and wattmeter. If the pointer of Wattmeter (#1) is below zero then, reverse the current leads (amps) of Wattmeter (#1). Then subtract the reading of Wattmeter (#1) from the reading of Wattmeter (#2) to get the true power measurement (WT). As the load is applied the value of Wattmeter (#1) will go down. When the load value is zero turn off the motor and wattmeter, reverse the current leads again. Don’t turn on the wattmeter until the load is equal to or greater then the load when the load value reached zero.

If the pointer of Wattmeter (#2) is below zero then, reverse the current leads (amps) of Wattmeter (#2). Then subtract the reading of Wattmeter (#2) from the reading of Wattmeter (#1) to get the true power measurement (WT). As the load is applied the value of Wattmeter (#2) will go down. When the load value is zero turn off the motor and wattmeter, reverse the current leads again. Don’t turn on the wattmeter until the load is equal to or greater then the load when the load value reached zero.

Graphing with Microsoft Excel.

Example from Lab-4: Step 13 tells you to plot VA and VG on the Y-axis versus IL on the X-axis. You should do this with a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. Put IL in the first column, then Excel Will use it as the x-axis. See sample spreadsheet and chart below. To draw this chart, do the following:

  • Type in the data with IL in Column A.
  • Type in VA and VG in Columns B and C.
  • Highlight the cells that contain your data.
  • Click on the Insert tab,
  • Choose Scatter Chart.
  • Choose the specific scatter graph style (smooth line).
  • If the Chart Wizard selects the row numbers instead of the data values do the following. Click on the chart select Chart Tools tab.
    • Click on Select Data tab.
      • Select the column A (Load Current (IL)) and push the Switch Row/Column button.
    • If the chart is showing just whole numbers.
      • Right click on the X-axis select Format axis… change Major Units: from Auto to fixed at 0.5
  • To add axis titles click the Layout tab in the Chart Tools tab.
    • Axis Titles
      • Primary Horizontal Axis Title
        • Tile Below Axis
      • Primary Vertical Axis Tile
        • Rotated Title
  • In the Labels tab select Chart Tile to add chart title.

Motor Theory — build intuition

Interactive models. Every widget is labeled Theoretical model, not measured data. Equations are cited. Where Jon’s Lab 1–6 points exist, overlays are optional and never alter his values. Each slider names the datasheet line it represents. Prefer citations to Jon’s Drive books when book_sources.json is available; until then manufacturer/university sources used below are marked, with book citation pending.

How to use: start with the question on each card → follow “Try this” → read “What you should notice” → connect to your datasheet.

Sources list (theory)

  1. maxon “Key information on maxon DC motor / EC motor” (May 2009 ed., UBC mirror PDF) — speed-torque line, η_max=1−√(I₀/I_A), M_H, M_R=k_M·I₀, P_max ≠ η_max.
  2. FAULHABER Technical Information DC-Motors — k_n, k_E, k_M, τ_m=R·J/k_M², R_th.
  3. MIT OCW 6.061 Chapter 11 (Kirtley) — V_a=R_a I_a+GΩI_f, shunt/series/compound, series runaway, commutator.
  4. NEMA MG-1 §1.43 speed regulation of DC motors; §1.44 voltage regulation of DC generators (NEMA Part 1 PDF).
  5. Oriental Motor Technical Manual Stepper Motor Edition — eqs. (3.2)(4.1)(4.7)(5.7), pull-in/out.
  6. TI SLVA321A Current Recirculation and Decay Modes; ADI Trinamic AN-026 / AN-003.
  7. SIU ECE 332A Lesson 22 — self-excited buildup & critical field resistance.
  8. Book citation pending — Chapman / Fitzgerald & Kingsley / Hughes / Kenjo slots for v2.3 via book_sources.json.

      From Lab to Datasheet

      Goal: take any motor, run the tests in this manual, and produce a complete datasheet from the results. The interactive template below uses schema datasheet_schema.json (157 parameters × 6 motor types from datasheet_template_and_test_map.md; 21 distinct manufacturer parts in the research matrix — Pittman DC030C listed twice in the raw 22-row sheet).

      Every exported field carries a provenance tag: measured / entered / computed (with formula) / cited / example_jon2012 / not_covered / blank. Hooks Compare to market and Export as build spec now open the v2.3 two-direction workflow (market, build spec) with the same schema plus the requirement provenance kind.

      Methods of Analysis — getting from a lab bench to a datasheet row

      ECET 231 companion module. Built 2026-11-04 18:52 America/Chicago. Every method below says what decision or datasheet row it produces, what data it needs, the formula, a worked example on Jon's own 2012 measurements, how sure the answer is, how to accept or reject it, the usual traps, and which datasheet-schema field it fills.

      Where every number comes from: measured — Jon 2012 (example_jon2012)computed with the formula shownentered by you (slider / box)citedTheoretical model

      Data-integrity rule used throughout. Jon's handwritten readings are the source of truth. This module never changes, replaces or "fixes" them. When a reading or a reduced value looks inconsistent, it is flagged with the check that found it, and the original value stays in every table and plot.
      1 · Engineering workflow spine (V-model) 1a · Design of experiments 1b · Measurement & uncertainty 1c · Data integrity & provenance 2 · Model ladder: ideal → full model 3 · Data reduction: least squares, residuals, limits 4 · Lab methods (losses, efficiency, OCC, regulation, IM tests, inertia, thermal, stepper) 5 · Mechanical loads: types, operating point, stability, acceleration, duty 6 · Sensitivity & tolerance: worst case, RSS, Monte Carlo 7 · Verification checklist & design-review gates 8 · Findings on Jon's data (flags only) 9 · Sources

      1 · The engineering workflow spine

      Requirements→Test plan→Measurement→Data reduction→Model fit→Verification→Report / datasheet

      The systems-engineering "Vee" pairs each step on the way down (deciding what is needed) with a step on the way up (proving it was delivered): it works by "associating each development stage with a corresponding testing stage" [INCOSE SEH 5e, p.35]. Verification is "objective evidence" that a requirement is met [INCOSE SEH 5e, p.138], by one of four methods — inspection, analysis, demonstration or test [INCOSE SEH 5e, p.139]; validation asks whether the motor does the job the user actually needs [INCOSE SEH 5e, p.146]. Traceability is the thread that ties each requirement to the test that verifies it [INCOSE SEH 5e, p.201].

      Left side of the Vee (define)Example in this courseRight side (prove)Verification methodEvidence in Jon's 2012 lab
      Stakeholder need"Drive a load at ~1700 rpm from a 115 V dc bus"ValidationDemonstrationLab 5 motor ran the Prony-brake load (p.29)
      Requirement (datasheet row)Speed regulation ≤ x %, η ≥ y % at rated load (wou_sr, wou_eta_max)Acceptance testTestLab 5 Table 1, rows 0 and 10 (p.29)
      Model / design analysisKΦ, Ra, loss model, load lineModel verificationAnalysis (residuals vs data)Model ladder against Lab 5 (§2)
      Test planWhich loads, how many points, replicates, instrument rangesData-reduction checkInspection + analysisLab 6 reduction audit (§8)
      Instrument selectionMeter class and range chosen for the expected readingUncertainty budgetAnalysis§1b, §6

      Design reviews are the checkpoints between these steps: "Technical reviews and audits are used to assess technical progress… and determine the technical status" [INCOSE SEH 5e, p.31]. Section 7 turns them into gates you can tick off.

      1a · Design of experiments (DOE) — plan before you measure

      • Controlled experiment. Change one input on purpose and hold the rest; it is the only way to get cause and effect rather than a coincidence [Navidi 3e, p.12].
      • Range and spread. Spread the x-values widely — a slope is pinned down best by the ends — but do not go "outside the range for which the linear model holds" [Navidi 3e, p.542]. Lab 5 loaded the motor from 0 to 240 in-oz in 11 equal steps (p.29): good spread, and it stops near the 3.5 A nameplate current.
      • Randomize order where drift (warm-up, line voltage) could masquerade as an effect; the definition of a completely randomized experiment is in [Navidi 3e, p.660]. A load sweep run only upward confounds load with warm-up time: take a second sweep downward, or randomize.
      • Replicate. Units given the same treatment are replicates [Navidi 3e, p.696]; repeat at least the no-load and the rated point so that a Type A spread exists.
      • Increasing and decreasing sweeps separate hysteresis from noise — Lab 3 did exactly this for the magnetization curve (p.23).
      • Write the reduction formula before the test. Then you know which readings you need (Lab 3 did not record generator speed, so its OCC cannot be moved to another speed with certainty — see §4).

      1b · Measurement & uncertainty

      Every reading is "Measured value = true value + bias + random error" [Navidi 3e, p.165]. Two ways to estimate the random part:

      • Type A — statistics on repeated readings: u = s/√n; least-squares slope and intercept standard errors are also Type A [NIST TN1297 Type A — web].
      • Type B — everything else: instrument specification, resolution, calibration certificate. Limits ±a with no other information → rectangular, u = a/√3 [NIST TN1297 Type B — web]. An analog meter specified to a % of full scale has a limiting error δA = class × full scale [Purkait EEMI, PDF p.38]; for the book's 0–25 A, 1 % ammeter reading 10 A that is ±0.25 A = ±2.5 % of the reading [Purkait EEMI, PDF p.38]. Read near full scale.
      • Combine independent components by root-sum-square, the law of propagation of uncertainty [NIST TN1297 combining — web]: uc² = Σ (∂f/∂xi)² ui² (Navidi eq. 3.12 [Navidi 3e, p.186]). A constant times a reading scales its uncertainty ([Navidi 3e, p.171]); a sum of independent readings adds in quadrature ([Navidi 3e, p.171]).
      • Report the expanded uncertainty U = k·uc, k = 2 for about 95 % [NIST TN1297 coverage — web], with no more than two significant digits in U [Navidi 3e, p.180], and round the value to the same decimal place.
      • Not independent? Use the conservative sum Σ|∂f/∂xi|ui [Navidi 3e, p.189] — this is the linear worst case used in §6.

      W1 · Instrument uncertainty calculator

      calculator

      How sure is one meter reading — and what range setting makes it surer?

      What to notice: the absolute limiting error depends only on the range, so the relative error explodes when the needle sits low on the scale. Type A only appears once you type repeated readings.
      Try this: keep reading = 10 A and change full scale 25 → 50 A. The ±% doubles. Then type five repeat readings to see Type A and Type B combine.
      Tie-back to the lab: Lab 5 armature current spans 0.5–3.6 A (p.29). On a 5 A range at 1 % FS the 0.5 A no-load reading carries ±10 % — the single largest relative uncertainty in the no-load loss estimate (§4, M1).

      1c · Data integrity & provenance

      1. Raw data are immutable. Keep the handwritten sheet (or its exact transcription) untouched; every derived table is a new table that points back to it (here: v2/graphs_data.py → manual page).
      2. Provenance on every number: measured / computed (with formula) / entered / cited. The colour legend at the top of this module is that rule made visible.
      3. Never fit-correct a measurement. A model may be fitted to the data; the data are never moved toward the model. Residuals are reported, not removed.
      4. Outliers are flagged, not deleted: "An outlier should not be deleted, however, unless there is reasonable certainty that it results from an error" [Navidi 3e, p.17]; deleting points for a nicer plot under-states the variability [Navidi 3e, p.513].
      5. Uncertain handwriting is carried as a note beside the value (see the transcription QA notes in §8), never silently resolved.
      6. Re-derive reduced columns from raw columns and compare — the Lab 6 audit in §8 found two formula issues this way.

      2 · Progressive model ladder — add one physical effect at a time

      Start with the simplest model that could work, compare it with the measurements, and add one effect only when the residuals say it is missing. The dc machine relations used are E = KΦω and T = KΦIa [Krause 3e, p.385] [Nise 7e, p.79] [Nise 7e, p.79]; the shunt-motor speed equation is in [Krause 3e, p.388]; saturation of the field is the magnetization curve [Krause 3e, p.11] [El-Sharkawi, p.122].

      5Thermal R(T)Ra(T) = Ra,25(234.5 + 25 + ΔT)/(234.5 + 25) [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.10 — web]ΔT entered; 25 °C reference assumed
      6Saturation + armature reactionKΦ = Ke·EOCC(IF)/EOCC(IF0)·(1 − karIA)OCC = Lab 3 (p.23); kar slider [citation pending]
      7Full modelall of the above, kar fitted by least squares on speedfitted parameter, data unchanged

      W2 · Model ladder against Lab 5 (shunt motor, p.29)

      Theoretical modelexample_jon2012 · p.29, p.27, p.23

      Which physical effect explains why the measured speed droops less than the simple Ra model predicts?

      What to notice: with the speed RMS residual held against the ladder, rung 1 (Ra) over-predicts droop at heavy load — the measured speed at 3.6 A is higher than (V − IR)/KΦ allows. Rungs 3–4 change nothing in steady state (they only set time constants). The thermal rung makes it worse (hot Ra means more droop, not less). Only a falling flux (lower IF on the saturated OCC, and armature reaction) raises the speed back: rung 6 halves the residual, rung 7 roughly quarters it.
      Try this: at rung 5 drag ΔT to 60 °C and watch the speed residual grow. At rung 6 drag kar from 0 up: the residual reaches a minimum near the rung-7 fitted value, then rises again (over-fitting the flux drop).
      Tie-back to the lab: the computed flux constant KΦ = (VA − IARa)/ω falls from 0.6003 V·s/rad at no load to 0.5623 at 3.6 A. The Lab 3 OCC explains part of this (IF fell from 0.33 to 0.31 A); the rest is armature reaction. Datasheet rows: wou_k_n_k_e, wou_k_m_k_t, wou_r, wou_tau_m, wou_tau_e.

      3 · Data reduction — least squares with honest error bars

      Method: straight-line least squares with slope/intercept uncertainty

      1. Desired outcome. A datasheet constant with ± (Kt, speed–torque gradient, R, critical field resistance) and a defensible range of validity.
      2. Method. Ordinary least squares, residual plot, standardized-residual flagging, interpolation-only predictions [Navidi 3e, p.539].
      3. Data needed. ≥ 5 (x, y) pairs spread over the range of use; the instrument class of both meters.
      4. Steps.b1 = Sxy/Sxx b0 = ȳ − b1·x̄ s² = Σe²/(n − 2) s_b1 = s/√Sxx s_b0 = s·√(1/n + x̄²/Sxx) R² = Sxy²/(Sxx·Syy) standardized residual e_i/(s·√(1 − h_i)), flag |·| > 2 (flag only)
      5. Worked example (Jon, Lab 5 p.29). Torque (in-oz × 0.0070616 = N·m) against armature current: slope Kt = 0.537 ± 0.018 N·m/A, intercept −0.221 ± 0.039 N·m, R² = 0.990; no point flagged. Speed against torque: gradient −99.6 ± 3.3 rpm/(N·m); the no-load point is flagged (standardized residual > 2) and kept.
      6. Uncertainty. Quote b1 ± 2sb1 for ≈95 %. The fit uncertainty adds to (does not replace) the instrument Type B uncertainty from §1b.
      7. Acceptance. Residual plot shows no curve or funnel [Navidi 3e, p.560]; R² is not enough on its own; every flagged point has a written explanation or stays as-is.
      8. Pitfalls. Extrapolating (stall torque from a no-load-to-rated sweep); forcing the line through zero when physics says there is an offset (friction makes T = Kt(I − I0)); deleting the awkward point.
      9. Datasheet field. wou_k_m_k_t (slope), wou_m_r friction torque (−intercept), wou_dn_dm (speed–torque gradient), wou_i_0.
      Why Kt (slope) ≠ Ke (no-load KΦ): the slope 0.537 N·m/A is about 10 % below the no-load KΦ 0.600 V·s/rad. In SI units the two constants are the same quantity [Nise 7e, p.79], so the gap is evidence for the flux falling with load (rung 6 of §2), not a measurement error.

      W3 · Least-squares fit, residuals and the extrapolation fence

      example_jon2012

      How well do Jon's points pin down the constant, and where does the straight line stop being trustworthy?

      What to notice: the shaded band is the measured x-range. Move the prediction point outside it and the verdict turns to EXTRAPOLATION; the standard error of the line grows with distance from x̄.
      Try this: pick "Lab 3 OCC" and raise "points used" from 3 to 7: the slope (critical field resistance) drops and R² falls as saturation bends the curve. Pick "Lab 1 resistor" and compare 1/slope with the 105 Ω Jon used in the power calculation (§8).
      Tie-back to the lab: every dataset here is a table from the 2012 manual, used unchanged. Flagged points stay in the fit and in the plot.

      4 · Lab methods — one card per datasheet row

      M1 · Separation of losses (no-load / Swinburne-style) and efficiency, direct vs indirect

      1. Desired outcome. Efficiency at the load points and maximum efficiency (wou_eta_max, dc _eta, ac _eta); the friction + core ("rotational") loss.
      2. Method. Direct (input–output): η = Pout/Pin with Pout = T·ω measured on the brake. Indirect (loss segregation): Pout = Pin − ΣPloss, with the rotational loss taken from a no-load run (the Swinburne idea [citation pending]). For induction motors IEEE 112 defines efficiency as output/input with output = input − losses [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.33 — web], limits the input–output method to machines under 1 kW [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.34 — web], and takes friction & windage as the zero-voltage intercept of the no-load loss line [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.13 — web]. The dc-machine counterpart is IEEE Std 113 [citation pending]. Power-flow definition: [Gieras 2e, p.130].
      3. Data needed. VA, IA, IF, speed and torque at each load; one no-load row; Ra (ideally hot).
      4. Steps.P_in = V_A·(I_A + I_F) (shunt field across V_A) P_rot,0 = (V_A0 − I_A0·R_a)·I_A0 (no-load row: all armature power is rotational loss) P_out,indirect = P_in − I_A²R_a − V_A·I_F − P_rot,0 P_out,direct = T[in-oz]·0.0070616·ω, ω = 2πn/60 η = P_out/P_in
      5. Worked example (Jon, Lab 5 p.29; Ra = 3.7 Ω from the Lab 4 sheet p.27, same machine — confirmed by Jon 2026-11-04). Prot,0 = (115 − 0.5·3.7)·0.5 = 56.6 W. Last row (3.6 A, 1625 rpm, 240 in-oz): direct η = 0.677, indirect η = 0.675. Transformer (Lab 2, pp.17–18): direct η = 72.32/80 = 0.904; Jon's indirect "90%" equals 72.32/(72.32 + 4 + 4) = 0.900, which uses the short-circuit copper loss unscaled; scaled to the load current (ideal-ratio primary current, an assumption) it gives 0.854.
      6. Uncertainty. Direct η at light load is dominated by the brake torque reading; indirect η by Prot,0, whose 0.5 A reading has the worst relative error (W1). The indirect method is more precise at high efficiency because it measures the small loss, not the difference of two large powers.
      7. Acceptance. Direct and indirect agree within their combined uncertainty at the rated point; any systematic gap is explained (stray load loss, Ra temperature).
      8. Pitfalls. Leaving out the field power; using a cold Ra; treating rotational loss as constant when speed falls a lot (compound motor); scaling copper loss with the wrong current.
      9. Datasheet field. wou_eta_max, dc _eta, ac _eta; loss table in the test report.

      W4 · Efficiency: direct vs indirect

      example_jon2012 · p.29, p.30, pp.17–18loss model

      Do two independent routes to efficiency agree on Jon's data?

      What to notice: at light load the two routes disagree most (small differences of large powers); at the last Lab 5 row they agree to within 0.002 (0.677 vs 0.675). The compound motor's indirect η is optimistic because its series-field loss is not in the data (series-field resistance not recorded).
      Try this: switch the rotational-loss model to "∝ speed" and change Ra ±0.5 Ω: which rows move? For the transformer, compare Jon's unscaled copper loss with the scaled one.
      Tie-back to the lab: Lab 5 recorded everything the indirect method needs except a hot Ra; the 3.7 Ω comes from the Lab 4 sheet; p.27 and p.29 are the same machine (confirmed by Jon 2026-11-04). The winding temperature at that reading was not recorded.

      M2 · Open-circuit characteristic (saturation) and critical field resistance

      1. Desired outcome. The magnetization curve (wou_graph_2, dc _graph), residual voltage (dc _v_res) and critical field resistance (dc _r_c): will a self-excited shunt generator build up?
      2. Method. Drive the machine at constant speed, separately excite the field, read E vs IF rising and falling [Krause 3e, p.11]. The air-gap (straight) part sets Rc; a shunt field line steeper than Rc cannot build up [citation pending]. Self-excited operation: [Krause 3e, p.387].
      3. Data needed. E and IF (both directions), the drive speed, field-circuit resistance.
      4. Steps.R_c ≈ slope of E vs I_F over the first k (linear) points (least squares, §3) field line: E = R_f·I_F ; build-up if R_f < R_c(n), R_c(n) = R_c(n0)·n/n0 (E ∝ n) no-load voltage = intersection of the field line with the OCC
      5. Worked example (Jon, Lab 3 p.23 and Lab 4 p.27). First 3 points: Rc = 300 ± 19 Ω. Lab 4 field circuit at no load: 139 V/0.56 A = 248 Ω < Rc, consistent with the generator building up to 139 V — if Lab 3 ran near 1800 rpm (its speed was not recorded).
      6. Uncertainty. sb1 of the slope; the unknown Lab 3 speed scales Rc directly (±5 % speed → ±5 % Rc) [citation pending].
      7. Acceptance. Rising and falling curves bracket each other (hysteresis), the linear region has ≥ 3 points, and the operating point is inside the measured IF range.
      8. Pitfalls. Lab 4's IF = 0.56 A lies outside Lab 3's measured 0–0.39 A, so the predicted no-load voltage is an extrapolation; reversing the field direction mid-test destroys the residual flux.
      9. Datasheet field. dc _graph, dc _r_c, dc _v_res, wou_r_f.

      W5 · OCC, field line and build-up

      example_jon2012 · p.23, p.27Theoretical model

      Will this generator build up, and to what voltage?

      What to notice: the field line through the origin cuts the OCC at the no-load voltage. Steepen it past the air-gap slope and the intersection disappears: no build-up.
      Try this: set the speed ratio to 0.8 (generator driven slower than in Lab 3) — Rc falls by 20 % and the 248 Ω field may no longer build up.
      Tie-back to the lab: Lab 4 shows the field circuit holding ≈ 237–260 Ω over its whole load sweep (VA/IF per row) — a built-in consistency check on Jon's readings.

      M3 · Speed regulation and voltage regulation

      1. Desired outcome. wou_sr speed regulation; dc _vr generator voltage regulation; transformer regulation.
      2. Method. Two-point definition at no load and at rated load. A shunt motor should change speed only slightly from no load to rated [Krause 3e, p.388]; a compound motor droops much more [Krause 3e, p.390].
      3. Data needed. No-load and rated-load speed (or voltage); the rated current from the nameplate (DM-100A: 3.5 A, p.8).
      4. Steps.SR = (n_NL − n_FL)/n_FL × 100 % VR = (V_NL − V_FL)/V_FL × 100 % rated point by interpolation in I_A (never extrapolate)
      5. Worked example (Jon). Shunt (p.29) no-load 1800 → last row 1625 rpm: SR = 10.8 %; compound (p.30) 1800 → 1170 rpm: 53.8 %. The last rows are at 3.6 A and 3.0 A, so W6 also interpolates both to the same current. Transformer: (221.5 − 226)/226 = −2.0 % — negative, flagged (§8).
      6. Uncertainty. Tachometer resolution dominates; SR is a small difference of two large numbers, so ±5 rpm on each reading gives about ±0.5 % absolute on the shunt SR.
      7. Acceptance. Same field setting and supply voltage for both points; rated point interpolated, not extrapolated.
      8. Pitfalls. Supply voltage sagging with load (Lab 5 VA fell 115 → 109 V, which inflates the droop); comparing machines at different currents.
      9. Datasheet field. wou_sr, dc _vr, dc _graph_2.

      W6 · Regulation at a chosen load

      example_jon2012 · p.29, p.30, p.27, pp.17–18

      What regulation does each machine show at the same current?

      What to notice: moving the "full-load" current beyond the last measured row turns the verdict to EXTRAPOLATION — the value is still printed, but it is not a measurement.
      Try this: set the current to 3.5 A (nameplate) and compare shunt vs compound; then look at the generator curve's collapse beyond about 3.3 A (p.27).
      Tie-back to the lab: Lab 4's terminal voltage falls 139 → 58 V while the load current stops rising at 3.3 A — the classic shunt-generator breakdown, measured.

      M4 · Induction-motor equivalent circuit from no-load and locked-rotor tests; two-wattmeter power factor

      1. Desired outcome. ac _equivalent_circuit_r1_r2_x1_x2_xm, no-load current ac _i_0, power factor ac _pf.
      2. Method. IEEE 112 derives the circuit "from test data recorded during a no-load test… and one of the impedance tests" [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.25 — web]; the impedance test is a locked-rotor test "at reduced voltage at rated frequency resulting in approximately rated current" [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.26 — web]. The no-load test runs uncoupled at rated voltage [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.12 — web]; its current is the average of the line currents [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.12 — web]; its input is all loss [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.13 — web]. Two-wattmeter power: the sum is total power, balanced or not [Purkait EEMI, PDF p.269]; power factor from the readings (Purkait eq. 7.34; IEEE 112 eq. 60 [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.32 — web]): equal readings ⇒ unity [Purkait EEMI, PDF p.272], one zero ⇒ 0.5 [Purkait EEMI, PDF p.272].
      3. Data needed. Line voltage, the three (or two) line currents, both wattmeter readings, at no load and locked rotor; DC stator resistance R1.
      4. Steps (per-phase wye equivalent).P = W1 + W2 PF_VA = P/(√3·V_L·I_L) PF_2W = cos(tan⁻¹(√3(W1 − W2)/(W1 + W2))) no load: Z0 = (V_L/√3)/I0, R0 = P0/(3I0²), X0 = √(Z0² − R0²) ≈ X1 + Xm locked: Zlr = (V_L/√3)/Ilr, Rlr = Plr/(3Ilr²) = R1 + R2', Xlr ≈ X1 + X2' (split 50/50 unless the design class says otherwise) Xm = X0 − X1
      5. Worked example (Jon, Lab 6 no-load row, pp.32–33). VL = 204 V, IL = 1.275 A, W1 + W2 = −68 + 182 = 114 W ⇒ Z0 = 92.4 Ω, R0 = 23.4 Ω, X0 = 89.4 Ω per phase (stator drop neglected). PF = 114/(√3·204·1.275) = 0.253; from the two readings 0.255 — the two routes agree. No locked-rotor test was run in 2012: enter one in W7 to finish the circuit.
      6. Uncertainty. At low PF one wattmeter reads negative and small errors in W1 − W2 dominate; R0 is a small resistive part of a large impedance, so its relative uncertainty is several times that of P.
      7. Acceptance. PF from W1/W2 agrees with P/(√3VI) within the meter uncertainty; three line currents within a few % (balanced supply).
      8. Pitfalls. Dropping the √3 (§8 shows this produced power factors above 1 in the 2012 reduction); forgetting the negative sign of a reversed wattmeter; using a single line current instead of the average.
      9. Datasheet field. ac _equivalent_circuit_r1_r2_x1_x2_xm, ac _i_0, ac _pf, ac _i_lr.

      W7 · Induction-motor test reduction

      example_jon2012 · pp.32–33 (no-load row)locked-rotor: entered

      What equivalent circuit do the no-load and locked-rotor readings imply?

      What to notice: with the locked-rotor sliders at 0 the module says so and computes only the no-load branch — it does not invent locked-rotor data.
      Try this: set W2 to 0 and W1 to the total: PF reads 0.5 exactly (Purkait's special case). Make W1 = W2: PF = 1.
      Tie-back to the lab: the defaults are Jon's no-load row from Lab 6. Running a reduced-voltage locked-rotor test in a future lab completes ac _equivalent_circuit_r1_r2_x1_x2_xm.

      M5 · Coast-down (retardation) test for inertia

      1. Desired outcome. Rotor (or rotor + load) inertia J (wou_j, ac _j), needed for τm and acceleration time.
      2. Method. Cut the supply and record speed vs time. With no electrical torque, the loss torque decelerates the inertia: Tloss = −J dω/dt — the inertia-torque equation Ti = J dω/dt [El-Sharkawi, p.319] with the developed torque set to zero [citation pending].
      3. Data needed. Speed vs time just after cut-off (tachometer + phone video, or a logged tach); the rotational loss at that speed from a no-load run.
      4. Steps.T_loss(n) = P_rot(n)/ω dω/dt = slope of ω(t) near n (least squares on a short window) J = −T_loss/(dω/dt)
      5. Worked example (Jon's loss, your slope). Lab 5 gives Prot,0 = 56.6 W at 1800 rpm ⇒ Tloss = 56.6/188.5 = 0.300 N·m (computed). No coast-down was recorded in 2012; enter a measured deceleration in W8.
      6. Uncertainty. u(J)/J = √[(uT/T)² + (uslope/slope)²]; take the slope over a window where Tloss is nearly constant.
      7. Acceptance. Repeat three times (replicates); J values within their combined uncertainty.
      8. Pitfalls. The shunt field must stay excited for a dc motor or the loss changes (no core loss); load coupling adds inertia and friction; brush friction varies with temperature.
      9. Datasheet field. wou_j, ac _j, wou_tau_m.

      W8 · Inertia from a coast-down

      slope: enteredloss: p.29

      How big is J if the motor slows at the rate you measured?

      What to notice: J is inversely proportional to the measured deceleration; a sloppy slope gives a sloppy J.
      Try this: halve the deceleration: J doubles, and the mechanical time constant τm = JRa/(KΦ)² that W2 and W11 use doubles with it.
      Tie-back to the lab: the loss torque comes from Jon's Lab 5 no-load row; adding a coast-down to a future Lab 5 completes wou_j.

      M6 · Thermal resistance and time constant from a heat run

      1. Desired outcome. wou_r_th1_r_th2 (K/W), wou_tau_w1_tau_w2, temperature rise ac _dt, and the hot Ra used by M1.
      2. Method. Load at constant loss until the temperature rise is constant [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.22 — web]; winding temperature by resistance, since conductor resistance rises with temperature [Purkait EEMI, PDF p.362], using IEEE 112 eq. (3) with k1 = 234.5 for copper [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.10 — web]. Fit ΔT(t) = ΔT∞(1 − e−t/τ) [Sudhoff PMD, p.354] [Sudhoff PMD, p.355] (v2.5: resolved with Sudhoff §10.2 — one thermal node is the first-order ODE C·dT/dt = P − ΔT/R, whose step response is this exponential; see Motor Models §5).
      3. Data needed. Cold resistance and its temperature; hot resistance (measured quickly after shutdown); loss power; ΔT vs time.
      4. Steps.t_hot = (R_hot/R_cold)(t_cold + 234.5) − 234.5 R_th = ΔT∞/P_loss τ from the fit (or the 63 % time)
      5. Worked example. Rcold = 3.7 Ω (Lab 4 sheet, temperature not recorded — 25 °C entered). A hot reading of 4.2 Ω would mean 25 + (4.2/3.7 − 1)(259.5) = 60.1 °C. No heat run was recorded in 2012 — the schema lists this as a gap test (Lab 12).
      6. Uncertainty. "a small error in measuring resistance will cause a comparatively large error in determining the temperature" [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.23 — web]: dT/dR = 259.5/3.7 = 70.1 °C per ohm, so ±0.01 Ω ⇒ ±0.7 °C. Use a 4-wire (Kelvin) measurement.
      7. Acceptance. Last readings change by ≤ the termination criterion; the exponential fit residuals show no trend.
      8. Pitfalls. Measuring R too late after shutdown (it cools fast); 2-wire leads adding tens of mΩ; mixing ambient changes into ΔT.
      9. Datasheet field. wou_r_th1_r_th2, wou_tau_w1_tau_w2, wou_t_max_class, ac _dt.

      W9 · Winding temperature by resistance + heat-run fit

      enteredTheoretical model

      How hot is the winding, and how fast does it get there?

      What to notice: a few hundredths of an ohm swing the computed temperature by degrees — the measurement of R is the whole test.
      Try this: paste readings from your own heat run (t in minutes, ΔT in °C); the fitted τ and ΔT∞ give Rth = ΔT∞/P.
      Tie-back to the lab: the rung-5 "thermal" step of W2 uses this same equation; Jon's Lab 5 data show a hotter Ra would make the speed residual worse, so temperature is not why the measured droop is small.

      M7 · Stepper pull-out curve reduction

      1. Desired outcome. ste_graph pull-out torque vs step rate; ste_f_s maximum starting frequency.
      2. Method. At each pulse rate raise the brake load until the motor loses step; that torque is the pull-out torque, "The torque just before asynchronism" [Oriental Motor Stepper Manual, p.43]; starting (pull-in) torque is the load it can start against [Oriental Motor Stepper Manual, p.41]. Scan rates finely around resonance [Oriental Motor Stepper Manual, p.37].
      3. Data needed. Pulse rate (pps), step angle, spring-scale force and pulley radius at the loss of synchronism.
      4. Steps.n [rpm] = f [pps] · θ_step[°]/360 · 60 T = F·r P = T·ω
      5. Worked example. No stepper data exist in the 2012 manual; enter your readings in W10. The reduction never smooths a dip — a dip at resonance is a result.
      6. Uncertainty. The breakaway force is read on a moving scale: take ≥ 3 replicates per rate; Type A from their spread.
      7. Acceptance. Curve is monotone except at identified resonances; replicate spread < 10 %.
      8. Pitfalls. Driving with a different supply voltage or microstep mode than the datasheet; including the inertia of the brake disk.
      9. Datasheet field. ste_graph, ste_graph_2, ste_f_s.

      W10 · Pull-out curve from your readings

      entered

      What pull-out curve do your readings give?

      Try this: change the step angle 1.8° → 0.9°: the same pps now means half the speed.

      5 · Mechanical loads — how the load decides where the motor runs

      El-Sharkawi writes the steady load torque as T = C·Tr(n/nr)k (eq. 1.1) and groups loads by k. The motor settles where its torque curve crosses the load curve; between those points the difference accelerates the inertia, Tm − TL = J dω/dt [El-Sharkawi, p.319].

      Load typeTL(ω)PowerExamplesSource
      Constant torque (k = 0)Tr∝ ωhoist, conveyor, positive-displacement pump[El-Sharkawi, p.7]
      Viscous / linear (k = 1)Tr·ω/ωr∝ ω²eddy-current brake, viscous frictioneq. 1.1 with k = 1 [El-Sharkawi, p.7]
      Fan / centrifugal pump (k = 2)Tr(ω/ωr)²∝ ω³fans, blowers, centrifugal pumps[El-Sharkawi, p.8]
      Constant power (k = −1)Trωr/ωconstantwinders, machine-tool spindles, saws[El-Sharkawi, p.8]
      InertialJ dω/dt (only while accelerating)transientflywheels, the Prony-brake drum itself[El-Sharkawi, p.319]
      PulsatingT̄ + ΔT·sin(θ)mean + ripplecompressors, piston pumps, crank pressesuse the mean for the operating point, Trms for heating (W12)
      Overhauling / regenerativenegative (load drives the shaft)flows back to the supplylowering a hoist, downhill vehiclemotor must brake; stability test still applies
      Reflected through a gearJeq = Jm + JL(nL/nm)²—gearbox, belt[El-Sharkawi, p.325]

      Steady-state stability and acceleration time

      Stability criterion. An equilibrium is stable "when an increase in speed causes load-torque to exceed the motor torque" [EEEGuide drive stability — web]:

      dT_L/dω > dT_m/dω at the operating point

      Check (web worked example [Skill-Lync worked example — web]): Tm = 1 + 2ω, TL = 3√ω ⇒ 4ω² − 5ω + 1 = 0 ⇒ ω = 0.25 (stable) and 1 rad/s (unstable). W11's solver reproduces both: 0.25 stable; 1.00 unstable.

      Acceleration (traveling) time, El-Sharkawi eq. 11.6:

      t = ∫ J dω/(T_m(ω) − T_L(ω)) from ω1 to ω2 (numerical trapezoid; infinite if T_m ≤ T_L on the way)

      For an unloaded dc motor this reduces to tst ≈ 3τ = 3JRa/(Kf)², independent of voltage [El-Sharkawi, p.328]; the book's Example 11.1 final speed (456 rpm) [El-Sharkawi, p.327], Example 11.4 [El-Sharkawi, p.329], Example 11.5 [El-Sharkawi, p.329] and the induction-motor Example 11.6 (tst ≈ 5.2 s) [El-Sharkawi, p.332] are reproduced by this module's code in QC.

      W11 · Operating point, stability and acceleration time

      Theoretical modeldc curve fitted to p.29

      Where does this motor settle with this load, is that point stable, and how long does it take to get there?

      What to notice: a dc shunt motor's falling line crosses any rising load once, stably. An induction motor has two regions: on the steep low-slip side it is stable; on the unstable side (left of the breakdown torque) a constant-torque load can sit at an unstable crossing. A load above the breakdown torque gives no crossing and the time becomes "stalls".
      Try this: choose the induction motor and a constant-torque load; raise Tr until the two crossings merge and vanish (breakdown). Then pick "web example" to see the 0.25 / 1.0 rad/s case.
      Tie-back to the lab: the dc curve is Jon's Lab 5 straight-line fit (n = 1789 − 99.6·T). Its stall end is an extrapolation far beyond the 0–1.7 N·m tested — labelled as such. The Prony brake is a friction (≈ constant-torque) load, which is why Lab 5 settled cleanly at every setting.

      Duty cycle and RMS-torque sizing

      Heating follows the RMS torque over a cycle, the "time-weighted average… of the torque during a complete machine cycle" [Yaskawa sizing (Design News 2009), p.2 — web]: each torque is squared, multiplied by its time, summed and divided by the cycle time [Linear Motion Tips RMS — web].

      T_rms = √( Σ T_i²·t_i / Σ t_i ) accept if T_rms ≤ continuous rating AND T_peak ≤ peak rating

      A stopped self-ventilated motor cools less well; some sizing guides de-rate rest time by a cooling factor — entered here as an assumption [citation pending].

      W12 · Duty-cycle Trms check

      entered profile

      Will the motor overheat on this accelerate–run–brake–rest cycle?

      What to notice: short, high acceleration torques barely move Trms but can exceed the peak rating; long run segments dominate Trms.
      Try this: lengthen the rest time: Trms falls. Then set the cooling factor below 1 and see the benefit shrink.
      Tie-back to the lab: the default continuous rating is the Lab 5 torque at 3.6 A (240 in-oz = 1.69 N·m, p.29) — an entered stand-in for a datasheet wou_m_n; replace it with the real rating.

      6 · Sensitivity & tolerance — worst case, RSS and Monte Carlo

      Method: three ways to put an error bar on a computed datasheet value

      1. Desired outcome. A ± on any reduced value (Ke, η, Rparallel) and the input that dominates it.
      2. Method. Worst case (all inputs at their limits in the worst direction; linear version Σ|∂f/∂x|u) [Navidi 3e, p.189]; RSS (independent inputs, eq. 3.12) [Navidi 3e, p.186]; Monte Carlo (sample the inputs, compute the spread). Navidi's comparison: both usually agree, simulation does not need small uncertainties, but propagation shows which input dominates [Navidi 3e, p.308].
      3. Data needed. The formula, each input's value and standard uncertainty (§1b).
      4. Steps.u_RSS = √Σ(∂f/∂x_i·u_i)² u_WC = Σ|∂f/∂x_i|·u_i share_i = (∂f/∂x_i·u_i)²/u_RSS² MC: draw x_i ~ N(x_i, u_i) N times (seeded), report mean, s, 2.5–97.5 % interval
      5. Worked example. Book check (Navidi Ex. 3.20 [Navidi 3e, p.188]): 100 ± 10 Ω ∥ 20 ± 1 Ω = 16.67 ± 0.75 Ω (RSS), conservative 0.97 Ω. On Jon's Lab 5 no-load row KΦ = 0.6003 V·s/rad; with the entered meter classes in W13 the Ra term is negligible at no load and speed + voltage dominate.
      6. Uncertainty. MC sampling error ∝ 1/√N; the seed is fixed so results are reproducible.
      7. Acceptance. RSS ≈ MC (if not, the function is strongly non-linear over the input spread — use MC); worst case used only where inputs may be correlated or where safety demands it.
      8. Pitfalls. Treating a % of full-scale spec as % of reading; adding uncertainties linearly and calling it RSS; reporting U with 4 significant digits.
      9. Datasheet field. The "±" column of every reduced row; tolerance band on wou_k_n_k_e, wou_eta_max.

      How this module relates to the rest of the manual: the steady-state model ladder fitted to Jon's Lab 5 data is in Methods of Analysis §2, single-exponential heat-run fitting in § thermal, coast-down in § coast-down, the RMS-torque duty rule in § duty cycle, and speed/current control loops in the Control Theory module. This module adds the dynamics (state-space ODEs), the impedance view (what an LCR meter or VNA sees), the parasitic capacitances behind PWM common-mode and bearing currents, the BLDC mapping, and thermal behaviour written as differential equations. Lab procedures: Lab 8 winding R & L, Lab 9 Ke/Kt, Lab 10 no-load / locked rotor, Lab 11 inertia & time constants, Lab 12 thermal; datasheet: lab → datasheet map.

      1 · One model for brushed dc and BLDC

      A brushed dc motor and a BLDC motor convert energy by the same two relations: back-EMF proportional to speed and torque proportional to current [Krause 3e, p.385] [Nise 7e, p.79] [Nise 7e, p.79] [Gieras 2e, p.129] [Mohan PE1, p.175]. The difference is who commutates: in the brushed machine the commutator and brushes switch the armature coils mechanically; in the BLDC machine an inverter switches the phases electronically using rotor-position (Hall) signals. A permanent-magnet dc machine is described by the shunt-machine equations with constant field [Krause 3e, p.396], and Krause shows that a PM ac machine fed in step with rotor position has dc-motor-like terminal characteristics [Krause 3e, p.130], written va = raIa + ωrkv [Krause 3e, p.129]. Xia makes the same reduction for 120° (two-phase-on) conduction: two phases in series behave as one dc armature with ra = 2R, La = 2(L − M) and line back-EMF coefficient ke [Xia BLDC, p.40].

      QuantityBrushed dc (PM or shunt, constant field)BLDC, six-step 120° (Xia)BLDC/PMSM, sinusoidal (FOC, Krause qd)
      ResistanceRa between brushes (includes brush drop unless separated, §4)ra = 2R (line-to-line)rs per phase
      InductanceLaLa = 2(L − M)Lq, Ld (= Lls + Lm)
      EMF constantKe = KΦ [V·s/rad]ke line, flat top [V·s/rad]λ′m [V·s] per electrical rad/s, phase peak
      Torque constantKt = Ke in SIKT = ke (eq. 2.21)Te = (3/2)(P/2)λ′m iq
      Commutationcommutator + brushesHall sensors → 6 inverter statesencoder/observer → Park transform → PWM
      Extra parasiticsbrush drop, armature reaction, commutation sparkingmutual M, EMF shape, commutation torque ripplesaliency Ld ≠ Lq, PWM common-mode, bearing currents

      What to notice: everything in rungs 1–3 below is written for the dc armature; for a BLDC motor driven six-step, use the line-to-line values (ra, La, ke) and the same equations apply between commutation events. For FOC, §6 gives the qd equations and the exact √3, 2/3 and 3/2 factors.

      2 · Rung 1 — the LR armature, back-EMF and the mechanical J–B

      2.1 Locked rotor: the LR circuit alone

      With the shaft blocked, ω = 0 and the back-EMF is zero, so the armature is a series R–L:

      L di/dt + R i = v(t) step v = V: i(t) = (V/R)·(1 − e^(−t/τe)), τe = L/R

      Variables: i armature current [A]; v terminal voltage [V]; R armature resistance [Ω]; L armature inductance [H]; τe electrical time constant [s] (Krause's τa = LAA/ra [Krause 3e, p.395]). After one τe the current reaches 63 % of its final value [Nise 7e, p.162]. Identifies R and L: Lab 8 (fields bru_r, bru_l, bru_tau_e; wound-field wou_r, wou_l, wou_tau_e; BLDC bld_r_ll_l_ll, bld_tau_e).

      W1 · Locked-rotor current step (RK4 vs exact)

      ∿ modelR from p.27

      How long does the armature current take to build up, and is the solver right?

      What to notice: L is a blank entry — La was not measured in 2012. Until you enter it the widget shows only the final value V/R. With L entered, RK4 and the exact exponential agree to better than 10⁻⁶ relative.
      Try this: enter your Lab 8 inductance, then drop the RK4 step count to 4 per τe and watch the error grow (RK4 error ∝ h⁴).
      Tie-back: R = 3.7 Ω is the value written on Jon's Lab 4 sheet (p.27, same DM-100A machine as p.29). Whether it includes the brushes, and at what temperature it was read, is not recorded — see §9.

      2.2 Running: two coupled first-order ODEs

      Let the rotor turn. Kirchhoff's voltage law around the armature and Newton's law on the shaft give the PM (or constant-field) dc machine state equations [Krause 3e, p.397] in fundamental form px = Ax + Bu [Krause 3e, p.397]:

      L di/dt = v − R i − Ke ω J dω/dt = Kt i − B ω − T_L d/dt [ i ] [ −R/L −Ke/L ] [ i ] [ 1/L 0 ] [ v ] [ ω ] = [ Kt/J −B/J ] [ ω ] + [ 0 −1/J ] [ T_L ]

      Variables and units: ω shaft speed [rad/s]; Ke back-EMF constant [V·s/rad]; Kt torque constant [N·m/A] (numerically equal to Ke in SI [Nise 7e, p.79]); J rotor + load inertia [kg·m²]; B viscous friction [N·m·s/rad]; TL load torque [N·m]. Unit check: Keω is V·s/rad × rad/s = V; Kti is N·m/A × A = N·m; Bω is N·m. The block diagram is Krause Fig. 10.5-1 [Krause 3e, p.395].

      Transfer functions (Laplace transform with zero initial conditions):

      D(s) = (Ls + R)(Js + B) + Ke·Kt I(s)/V(s) = (Js + B)/D(s) Ω(s)/V(s) = Kt/D(s) Ω(s)/T_L(s) = −(Ls + R)/D(s) with B = 0: D(s) = LJ·[s² + s/τe + 1/(τe τm)], τe = L/R, τm = J R/(Ke Kt)

      τm = JR/(KeKt) is the mechanical time constant [s] (unit check: kg·m²·Ω/(V·s/rad · N·m/A) = s). The poles are s = −1/(2τe) ± √(1/(4τe²) − 1/(τeτm)): both real when τm ≥ 4τe (the usual case, and then τm and τe are roughly the two time constants), complex — an overshooting speed step [Nise 7e, p.174] — when τm < 4τe. Neglecting L gives Nise's first-order motor model [Nise 7e, p.80]. Steady state (d/dt = 0):

      ω_ss = (Kt V − R T_L)/(R B + Ke Kt) i_ss = (B V + Ke T_L)/(R B + Ke Kt)

      Assumptions of rung 1: linear magnetics (no saturation); constant flux (PM or constant field current); no brush drop; no armature reaction; friction purely viscous; R, Ke, Kt independent of temperature; no capacitance; ideal commutation. Each is removed in rung 2 or 3.

      W2 · Voltage step, eigenvalues and Bode plot of rung 1 [Nise 7e, p.531]

      ❝ Krause Ex. 10A presetJon preset (L, J blank)

      Given R, L, Ke, Kt, J and B, how do current and speed respond to a voltage step, and what do the transfer functions look like?

      What to notice: with the published Krause Example 10A motor [Krause 3e, p.392], rung 1 reproduces the book's no-load point and Example 10B load point [Krause 3e, p.393] from the steady-state formula, and its eigenvalues are complex: τm < 4τe, so the speed step overshoots slightly. The exact solution x(t) = xss + eAt(x₀ − xss) (2×2 matrix exponential, closed form) lies on top of the RK4 curve.
      Try this: switch to the Jon preset and enter your own La (Lab 8) and J (Lab 11). Watch the ratio τm/τe: below 4 the poles become complex.
      Tie-back: the Jon preset uses R = 3.7 Ω (p.27, measured), Ke = Kt = KΦ₀ = (VA − IARa)/ω = 0.6003 V·s/rad from the p.29 no-load row (computed), B = KΦ₀·IA0/ω₀ = 0.00159 N·m·s/rad (computed by Krause's Example 10A method [Krause 3e, p.392]), V = 115 V (p.29 row 0). La and J were not measured in 2012: blank.

      The mechanical side looks like a capacitor. Seen from the armature terminals, the motional term KeKt/(Js + B) is exactly the impedance of a capacitor Ceq = J/(KeKt) [F] in parallel with Req = KeKt/B [Ω] (derived here from D(s) above; unit check kg·m²/(V·s·N·m/A) = A·s/V = F). Inertia stores kinetic energy ½Jω² the way a capacitor stores ½CeqE² with E = Keω. That is the first "C" of the LRC rung: the running motor is an R–L in series with a parallel ReqCeq, and L with Ceq resonates at f₀ = (1/2π)√(KeKt/(LJ)), the electromechanical natural frequency of rung 1.

      3 · Rung 2 — LRC: what the capacitance physically is

      Two different capacitances appear once frequencies rise above the mechanical band:

      • Interturn and coil-to-coil capacitance Cp — adjacent turns and coils of the armature (or BLDC phase) separated by enamel form a distributed capacitance that, lumped, sits across the winding terminals [citation pending]. The analogous inter-layer and inter-winding capacitance of transformer windings governs their high-frequency transients [Sudhoff PMD, p.252]. With L it gives a parallel self-resonance fsr = 1/(2π√(LCp)); above fsr the winding looks capacitive.
      • Winding-to-frame capacitance Cwf (Csf, stator-to-frame, in the bearing-current literature) — the largest share of the motor's stray capacitance is between the stator windings and the frame [ABB Technical Guide No. 5, PDF p.14 — web] [Yaskawa AN.G7.02, PDF p.5 — web]. Brushed dc: terminal-to-frame [citation pending]. BLDC: phase-to-frame and phase-to-phase Cpp.
      • Rotor capacitances — stator-to-rotor Csr (small), rotor-to-frame Crf (typically about ten times Csr) [Yaskawa AN.G7.02, PDF p.5 — web], and the bearing oil-film capacitance Cb in parallel with Crf.
      Locked rotor: Z(jω) = [R + jωL] ∥ 1/(jωC_p) Running: Z(jω) = [R + jωL + (Z_m ∥ R_fe)] ∥ 1/(jωC_p), Z_m = Ke·Kt/(jωJ + B) = R_eq ∥ C_eq Self-resonance (R ≪ ωL): f_sr = 1/(2π√(L·C_p)) ⇒ C_p = 1/((2π f_sr)²·L)

      Rfe [Ω] is an equivalent iron-loss (eddy-current) shunt resistance, the same idea as the core-loss resistance R = v²/P of a transformer model [Sudhoff PMD, p.220]; on an impedance sweep it shows up as Re Z rising with frequency. The PWM drive is a fast voltage source: hard switching produces large dv/dt that couples through stray capacitance [Mohan PE1, p.164].

      W3 · Terminal impedance sweep: motional Ceq, interturn Cp, iron loss

      ❝ Krause Ex. 10A base○ Cp, Rfe entries

      What will the LCR meter / VNA show across the armature terminals, rotor locked and running?

      What to notice: rotor running, a peak appears at low frequency — the motional Req∥Ceq resonating with L. Rotor locked, the curve is R then ωL. Cp has no cited value: it stays blank until you enter one (or a measured fsr), and only then does the high-frequency resonance appear.
      Try this: enter Cp, then compare the computed fsr with the peak of your MM-T1 sweep pasted into the box.
      Tie-back: Jon owns both an LCR meter and a VNA; MM-T1 and MM-T3 (§7) turn this curve into the new v2.5 fields *_z_sweep, *_f_sr, *_c_p, *_r_fe.

      3.1 PWM common-mode voltage, frame current and shaft voltage

      A two-level inverter's three legs each sit at +Vdc/2 or −Vdc/2 with respect to the dc-link midpoint. The motor neutral (and through Cwf the frame and shaft) sees the average of the three, the common-mode voltage, which is not zero; it is proportional to the dc bus voltage at the switching frequency [ABB Technical Guide No. 5, PDF p.10 — web]:

      v_cm = (v_a0 + v_b0 + v_c0)/3 = V_dc·(S_a + S_b + S_c)/3 − V_dc/2 S_k ∈ {0,1} levels: −V_dc/2, −V_dc/6, +V_dc/6, +V_dc/2; each leg transition steps v_cm by V_dc/3 i_cm(t) = C_wf · dv_cm/dt peak ≈ C_wf·(V_dc/3)/t_r shaft voltage (capacitive divider, Cb in parallel with C_rf): v_shaft = v_cm · C_sr/(C_sr + C_rf + C_b)

      The current law is the one ABB states — each edge forces a current proportional to the voltage change through the earth capacitances [ABB Technical Guide No. 5, PDF p.11 — web]; the divider ratio (bearing voltage ratio) is derived here from the Yaskawa capacitance network [Yaskawa AN.G7.02, PDF p.5 — web]. When the shaft voltage exceeds the lubricant film's breakdown, the film discharges (EDM bearing current) [citation pending].

      W4 · Common-mode voltage, frame current and shaft voltage over one PWM period

      ∿ normalized to Vdc○ Vdc, Cwf entries

      How big are the common-mode steps, the frame current spikes and the shaft voltage for a given drive?

      What to notice: vcm never rests at zero — it jumps by Vdc/3 at every leg transition. The frame current is a train of spikes whose height depends on tr, not on the switching frequency. With Crf/Csr = 10 (Yaskawa's "typically about ten times") and Cb negligible, the shaft sees at most 1/11 of vcm.
      Try this: move tr across the 50–200 ns range given for IGBT drives [Skibinski et al., IEEE PCIC 1996, PDF p.3 — web] and watch the current peak scale as 1/tr.
      Tie-back: Jon's 2012 bench ran from dc supplies (no inverter), so there is no 2012 data here. MM-T2 measures Cwf with the LCR meter (*_c_wf), MM-T4 the drive rise time (*_t_rise_drive).

      3.2 The cable: distributed L and C, reflected wave

      The motor cable is a transmission line with surge impedance Z₀ = √(L′/C′) (L′, C′ per unit length), found to be relatively constant at 80 to 180 Ω for common cable types; the voltage at the motor is (1 + Γ) times the incident voltage with Γ = (Zload − Z₀)/(Zload + Z₀) [Skibinski et al., IEEE PCIC 1996, PDF p.2 — web]. Because a motor's high-frequency impedance is much higher than Z₀ [citation pending], Γ approaches 1 and the terminal voltage approaches 2 per unit. The paper's critical length is a quarter wavelength of the edge frequency fe = 1/(πtr): lc = 772.8·tr[µs] ft [Skibinski et al., IEEE PCIC 1996, PDF p.3 — web] — computed with the free-space speed of light; real cable is slower [citation pending].

      Lossless line, wave speed v, one-way delay T = ℓ/v, source reflection Γs, load reflection Γl, ramp edge r(t) (0→1 in t_r): v_motor(t) = (1 + Γl)·Σ_k (Γl·Γs)^k · r(t − (2k+1)T) (bounce-diagram sum, derived here) full (1 + Γl) overshoot needs the reflection back before the edge ends: 2T ≥ t_r ⇔ ℓ ≥ v·t_r/2

      W5 · Reflected wave at the motor terminals

      ❝ Z₀ range and tr range cited∿ Γ explorer

      At what cable length does the motor see close to twice the bus voltage?
