      W6 · Parasitic simulator (rung 3 on the Krause Example 10A motor)

      ❝ Krause Ex. 10A base∿ parasitic sliders start at zero

      Which parasitic changes the start-up transient, which changes the steady state, and by how much?

      What to notice: brush drop, Coulomb friction and temperature shift the steady state (the widget checks the simulated final values against the closed-form steady state with those terms moved to the inputs); saturation changes only the current rise; cogging adds a ripple at Ncog times the shaft frequency that is largest at low speed.
      Try this: raise Vb towards Gieras's 2 V on this 6 V motor: one third of the supply is lost at the brushes. Then add ΔT = 60 K and watch Ke(T) and R(T) push the speed in opposite directions.
      Tie-back: on Jon's DM-100A (115 V) the same 2 V would be under 2 % of the supply — a reason brush drop is usually folded into Ra on larger machines.

      W7 · Jon's Lab 5 (p.29): Coulomb or viscous friction?

      ● p.29 measuredƒ computed○ J entry

      Jon's no-load current is 0.50 A. Is the loss torque it represents Coulomb (constant) or viscous (∝ ω), and why does it matter for dynamics?

      What to notice: per row, loss torque Tloss = E·IA/ω − Tshaft (E = VA − IARa, power balance). Jon's speeds span only about 10 % (1625–1800 rpm), so a straight-line fit Tloss = Tc + Bω cannot separate the two terms: the fitted B comes out with a standard error as large as B itself (numbers below), so the data are consistent with almost pure Coulomb friction. Steady-state speed predictions of the three readings differ by only a few rpm — far less than the error from assuming constant flux, which is AM's armature-reaction finding — but their coast-downs differ completely.
      Try this: enter a J (Lab 11) to see the three coast-down predictions: viscous-only never quite stops (t5 % = (J/B)·ln 20), Coulomb-only stops linearly at t = Jω₀/Tc, combined stops at t = (J/B)·ln(1 + Bω₀/Tc).
      Tie-back: MM-T7 (coast-down, AM coast-down method) is the test that separates them → v2.5 wou_t_c, wou_b_v. The loss torque also contains armature reaction effects — see the flags.

      5 · Thermal models as differential equations

      A thermal node obeys conservation of energy: stored heat changes at the rate power goes in minus heat flows out. Sudhoff writes the mean temperature of a region as a state variable with a first-order ODE [Sudhoff PMD, p.355] [Sudhoff PMD, p.354], with thermal capacitance C = cρV [J/K] [Sudhoff PMD, p.350]; Mohan draws the same network as an electrical analogy (power ↔ current source, temperature ↔ voltage) [Mohan PE1, p.32].

      5.1 One node

      C_th·dθ/dt = P − θ/R_th, θ = T − T_amb [K], P loss [W], R_th [K/W], C_th [J/K] integrating factor e^(t/τ): θ(t) = P·R_th + (θ0 − P·R_th)·e^(−t/τ), τ = R_th·C_th [s], θ_ss = P·R_th unit check: K/W · J/K = J/W = s

      Published check (Sudhoff Example 10.2A): a 10 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm bar with c = 469 J/(kg·K), ρ = 7500 kg/m³, k = 16.7 W/(m·K), both ends held at 26 °C, sides insulated, 10 W dissipated [Sudhoff PMD, p.355] [Sudhoff PMD, p.356]. With RWx = l/(2kS) [Sudhoff PMD, p.353]: RWx = 7.485 K/W; C = cρV = 140.7 J/K; the steady mean rise from (10.2-6) is p·l²/(12k) = P·RWx/6 = 12.48 K, i.e. mean temperature 38.48 °C; as one node, τ = C·RWx/6 = 175.5 s. The book notes the lumped circuit and the PDE agree in the mean but not exactly.

      5.2 Two nodes (winding + housing): a matrix ODE

      C1·dθw/dt = P1 − (θw − θh)/R1 C2·dθh/dt = P2 + (θw − θh)/R1 − θh/R2 d/dt [θw] [ −1/(R1C1) 1/(R1C1) ] [θw] [P1/C1] [θh] = [ 1/(R1C2) −(1/R1 + 1/R2)/C2 ] [θh] + [P2/C2] eigenvalues λ1,2 = tr/2 ± √((tr/2)² − det), τ_i = −1/λ_i (always real and negative: the matrix is similar to a symmetric one) winding step (P2 = 0): θw(t) = a1(1 − e^(−t/τ1)) + a2(1 − e^(−t/τ2)), a1 + a2 = P1(R1 + R2)

      Identifying the network from a two-exponential heat run (derived here by matching θw(s)/P = (R1 + R2 + sR1R2C2)/(1 + s(R1C1 + R2C2 + R2C1) + s²R1R2C1C2) to Σ (ai/P)/(1 + sτi)):

      R_s = (a1 + a2)/P, N1 = (a1·τ2 + a2·τ1)/P, S = τ1 + τ2, Π = τ1·τ2 C1 = Π/N1, R1 = N1/(S − R_s·C1), R2 = R_s − R1, C2 = N1/(R1·R2)

      W8 · One-node and two-node thermal ODEs (RK4 vs exact)

      ❝ Sudhoff 10.2A preset∿ two-node normalized

      How do one and two time constants show up in a heat run, and does the solver match the analytic answer?

      What to notice: the two-node curve rises fast (winding τ₁) then creeps (housing τ₂); a single exponential fitted to it underestimates the final rise if the run is stopped early. The two-node mode is normalized: time in units of R1C1, rise in units of P(R1 + R2); it makes no claim about any motor.
      Try this: make C₂/C₁ large and watch τ₁, τ₂ separate; feed the curve to W11 and recover R1, R2, C1, C2.
      Tie-back: Lab 12 (procedure) fills wou_r_th1_r_th2, wou_tau_w1_tau_w2; v2.5 adds wou_c_th1_c_th2. Jon's 2012 sheets have no heat run.

      5.3 Electro-thermal coupling: a nonlinear ODE, fixed points and runaway

      The loss depends on temperature, so the thermal ODE is nonlinear [Sudhoff PMD, p.381] [Sudhoff PMD, p.381]:

      C_th·dθ/dt = g(θ) = P_in(θ) − θ/R_th constant current: P_in = I²·R0·(1 + α(θ + T_amb − T0)) (linear in θ) constant voltage (locked rotor): P_in = V²/(R0·(1 + α(…))) (falls with θ → self-limiting) constant torque, PM: I = T_L/(Kt0·(1 + β(…))), P_in = I²·R(θ) (β < 0 for magnets → rises faster) fixed points θ*: g(θ*) = 0. stability: dg/dθ(θ*) < 0 (perturbation δθ decays with τ' = −C_th/g'(θ*)) constant current, T_amb = T0: Γ = α·I²·R0·R_th, θ* = I²R0R_th/(1 − Γ), τ' = τ/(1 − Γ), runaway iff Γ ≥ 1 constant torque (linearized): Γ_T ≈ (α − 2β)·I²·R0·R_th

      W9 · Thermal runaway explorer (normalized) with Jon's operating point

      ∿ normalized● p.29 I, p.27 R○ Rth entry

      When does copper heating feed on itself, and how close is a given operating point?

      What to notice: the phase line g(θ̂) crosses zero with negative slope (stable) for Γ < 1; as Γ → 1 the crossing runs off to infinity and the time constant stretches as 1/(1 − Γ). Constant voltage always has a stable crossing. With β/α < 0 (magnets weakening) constant torque runs away at a smaller Γ.
      Try this: set β/α to about −0.52 — the ratio of a ferrite magnet's −0.20 %/°C to copper's α at 25 °C (computed from the cited coefficients, assuming Kt ∝ Br) — and find the new critical Γ.
      Tie-back: at Jon's heaviest p.29 load (IA = 3.6 A) with Ra = 3.7 Ω, I²R₀ = 47.95 W; with α = 1/(234.5 + 25) the constant-current runaway threshold is Rth* = 1/(α·I²R₀) = 5.41 K/W. The 25 °C reference is an assumption (the temperature at which 3.7 Ω was read is not recorded), and the shunt motor is not at constant current. Rth of the DM-100A is unknown: enter your Lab 12 value.

      5.4 Duty cycle: periodic steady state

      Power P for ton, zero for toff, period tp = ton + toff. Solve the one-node ODE piecewise and require θ at the end of a period to equal θ at its start (periodic steady state):

      on: θ(t) = PR + (θ_min − PR)e^(−t/τ) off: θ(t) = θ_max·e^(−t/τ) θ_max = PR·(1 − e^(−t_on/τ))/(1 − e^(−t_p/τ)), θ_min = θ_max·e^(−t_off/τ), mean = PR·D, D = t_on/t_p limits: t_p ≪ τ → θ_max → PR·D (RMS-power rule valid); t_on ≫ τ → θ_max → PR (no benefit from the off time)

      The RMS-torque sizing rule (AM duty cycle) is the tp ≪ τ limit of this equation.

      W10 · Duty-cycle ripple: exact periodic steady state vs RK4

      ∿ normalized

      How much hotter than the average does the winding get on an intermittent duty, and when is the RMS rule safe?

      What to notice: θmax/θmean → 1 only when the period is short compared with τ. RK4 run for many cycles converges on the exact θmax, θmin.
      Try this: keep D = 0.5 and raise ton/τ from 0.05 to 3.
      Tie-back: fills nothing new by itself; uses *_tau_w1_tau_w2 and *_s1_cont (duty rating) from Lab 12.

      5.5 Fitting Rth and Cth from heat-run data

      Single exponential T(t) = T₀ + θ∞(1 − e−t/τ) gives Rth = θ∞/P and Cth = τ/Rth (AM covers this fit: AM W9). The winding temperature can be read by the resistance method T = (R/R₀)(k₁ + T₀) − k₁ [IEEE Std 112-2004, p.10 — web]. Here the fit is extended to two exponentials and converted to the two-node network with the identities of §5.2.

      W11 · Heat-run fit: one or two exponentials → Rth, Cth

      ○ your heat-run data

      Given (time, temperature) pairs and the loss power, what are Rth, Cth — and does a second time constant improve the fit?

      What to notice: loading W8's normalized curve and fitting it returns the R1, R2, C1, C2 W8 used — a round-trip test of the fitter, not motor data.

      6 · BLDC: six-step vs FOC, Clarke/Park, and the Ke/Kt conventions

      6.1 Six-step (trapezoidal, 120° conduction)

      Three Hall sensors divide each electrical revolution into six 60° sectors; in each sector two phases conduct in series and the third floats. Xia's model assumes no saturation, eddy or hysteresis loss, no armature reaction, a 120° flat-top air-gap field, no cogging and ideal switches [Xia BLDC, p.33]; voltage, torque and motion equations form the BLDC ODE model [Xia BLDC, p.39]. With two phases on, the dc-motor equations hold with line values (§1) and Te = 2pψmi = KTi [Xia BLDC, p.39] [Xia BLDC, p.40]; the transfer function for control design follows directly [Xia BLDC, p.40]. Control is the usual cascade of an inner current/torque loop and an outer speed loop [Xia BLDC, p.83] (see Control Theory).

      Ud = ra·i + La·di/dt + ke·Ω, ra = 2R, La = 2(L − M), ke = 2p·ψm (Xia 2.25; p pole pairs, Ω mech. rad/s, ψm flat-top phase flux) Te = KT·i, KT = ke (SI, 120° conduction)

      6.2 FOC (sinusoidal): Clarke, Park and the qd ODEs

      Measured phase currents are turned into a stationary two-axis vector by a forward Clarke transformation [Pulle ACED, p.30], rotated into rotor coordinates (Park); the controller's ud, uq are rotated back by a reverse Park transformation [Pulle ACED, p.43]. Krause's transformation carries the constant 2/3 [Krause 3e, p.88]; with it, power is P = (3/2)(vqsiqs + vdsids + 2v0si0s) [Krause 3e, p.90], and the same 3/2 appears in the torque because amplitude-invariant space vectors are used [Pulle ACED, p.21] — it holds only for three-phase amplitude-invariant vectors [De Doncker 2e, p.99].

      Clarke (amplitude-invariant): f_α = (2/3)(f_a − f_b/2 − f_c/2), f_β = (f_b − f_c)/√3, f_0 = (f_a + f_b + f_c)/3 Park (Krause K_s, θ = θr): f_q = (2/3)[f_a cos θ + f_b cos(θ − 2π/3) + f_c cos(θ + 2π/3)] f_d = (2/3)[f_a sin θ + f_b sin(θ − 2π/3) + f_c sin(θ + 2π/3)] rotor-frame PM machine: L_q di_q/dt = v_q − r_s i_q − ω_r L_d i_d − ω_r λ'm L_d di_d/dt = v_d − r_s i_d + ω_r L_q i_q T_e = (3/2)(P/2)[λ'm i_q + (L_d − L_q) i_q i_d], J·(2/P)·dω_r/dt = T_e − B_m(2/P)ω_r − T_L, dθ_r/dt = ω_r applied voltages: v_as = √2·v_s·cos θ_ev (Krause 4.3-18) → V_qs = √2 v_s cos φ_v in the rotor frame

      Variables: ωr electrical rotor speed [rad/s] = (P/2)·ωrm; P number of poles; λ′m peak phase flux linkage of the magnet [V·s]; iq, id [A] are peak-phase-amplitude quantities (amplitude-invariant). Krause: stepped inverter voltages are approximated by their fundamental and Vqs = √2vscos φv [Krause 3e, p.127]; with φv = 0, Lq = Ld = Ls, Te = (3/2)(P/2)rsλ′m(Vqs − ωrλ′m)/(rs² + ωr²Ls²) — dc-motor-like if ωr²LqLd is small [Krause 3e, p.130].

      6.3 Mapping the brushed model: Ke and Kt conventions (√3, 2/3, 3/2, P/2)

      base: Ke_ph,pk = (P/2)·λ'm [V phase-peak per mech rad/s] Ke_ph,rms = Ke_ph,pk/√2 Ke_LL,pk = √3·Ke_ph,pk Ke_LL,rms = √3·Ke_ph,pk/√2 per 1000 r/min: multiply by 1000·2π/60 = 104.72 rad/s; peak-to-peak = 2 × peak torque: Te = (3/2)(P/2)λ'm·i_q = (3/2)·Ke_ph,pk·I_pk ⇒ Kt_pk = (3/2)·Ke_ph,pk [N·m per A phase-peak] Kt_rms = (3/√2)·Ke_ph,pk = √3·Ke_LL,rms [N·m per A rms] (sinusoidal, FOC, i_d = 0) trapezoidal 120° (Xia): flat-top phase EMF coefficient k_ph ⇒ ke(line) = 2·k_ph and KT = ke brushed dc: Kt = Ke (one number, SI)

      All the factors above are derived here from the cited Krause/Xia equations; manufacturer datasheets state Ke in any of these bases, which is why the v2.5 schema adds bld_ke_convention. Published check: Krause's example BLDC has 60 V peak-to-peak line-to-line open-circuit voltage at 1000 r/min, 4 poles, giving λ′m = 0.0827 V·s [Krause 3e, p.131]; the converter below recovers λ′m = 0.0827 V·s from 60 V p-p at 1000 r/min (formula: λ′m = (60/2)/√3 / (1000·2π/60·2)).

      W12 · Ke / Kt convention converter

      ❝ Krause BLDC check○ your datasheet value

      A datasheet says "Ke = … V/krpm": what is it per phase, per rad/s, and what Kt does it imply?

      What to notice: the same motor's "Ke" differs by √3 (line vs phase), √2 (peak vs rms), 2 (p-p vs peak), and 104.72 (krpm vs rad/s); Kt per rms ampere is √3 × KeLL,rms for a sinusoidal machine, while for a trapezoidal machine KT = ke(line).
      Try this: enter 60 (V p-p, line-line, per krpm) with 4 poles and read λ′m = 0.0827 V·s — Krause's number.
      Tie-back: bld_k_n_k_e, bld_k_m_k_t, bld_m_p (pole pairs) and v2.5 bld_ke_convention.

      W13 · BLDC/PMSM qd simulation: sinusoidal vs six-step voltage (Krause example machine)

      ❝ Krause §4.5 preset

      From standstill, how does the machine accelerate, and what does six-step voltage do to the torque?

      What to notice: with sinusoidal voltages (Krause's free-acceleration study [Krause 3e, p.131]) the speed settles at ωr = √2vs/λ′m when unloaded; the stall torque equals (4.5-5) at ωr = 0. Six-step 180° voltage with the same fundamental (Vdc = π√2vs/2) reaches nearly the same speed but adds torque ripple at 6× the electrical frequency. Power computed from abc quantities equals (3/2)(vqiq + vdid) at every step — a check of the 3/2.
      Try this: add a load torque and an advance angle φv; compare final speed and ripple between the two voltage modes.
      Tie-back: Ld, Lq for your motor: MM-T12 → bld_ld_lq. Limitation: 120° current-controlled trapezoidal commutation with a floating phase is not simulated here (only its line-value reduction, §6.1).

      • termframe-dc: Terminal-to-frame capacitance of a brushed dc motor specifically (the read sources treat ac/PWM motors): proposed test MM-T2.
      • zload: Motor surge impedance to fast edges: the read source says it is not well documented; to be measured (VNA, proposed test MM-T4).
      • vna-method: Standard method for motor winding impedance sweeps with an LCR meter / VNA (e.g. IEC/IEEE procedure): not read in this job.
      • brushres: Brush contact resistance as a nonlinear function of current density (Gieras Table 4.3 gives drops, not an R(i) law): citation pending.
      • cogging-model: Sinusoidal approximation T_cog = T_c,pk·sin(N_c θ) with N_c = LCM(slots, poles) periods per revolution: no owned page read with this formula.
      • arm-react-law: Linear flux-reduction law KΦ(i) = KΦ0(1 − k_ar·i) for armature reaction: a modelling choice made here, not a cited law.
      • sat-law: Incremental-inductance saturation law L(i) = L0/(1 + (i/I_sat)²): a modelling choice made here, not a cited law.
      • kt-temp-shunt: Shunt-field heating lowering I_F (and KΦ) at constant field voltage: follows from R(T) but no owned page quotes it for the DM-100A.
      • bearing-film: Bearing lubricant-film breakdown threshold voltage (EDM bearing current onset): not read.
      • v-cable: Wave speed in motor cable v = 1/√(L′C′) (slower than c): the read paper’s eq. (6) uses the free-space c; cable velocity factor not read.

      Lab - 7

      Stepper Motor Characteristics

      This lab was not part of the Summer 2012 printed manual. It follows the same Objective / Equipment / Safety / Procedure / Tables / Discussion / Graphs pattern as Labs 1–6.

      Objective:

      1. Identify stepper types (PM, variable reluctance, hybrid) and drive modes (full / half / microstep; chopper vs L/R).
      2. Measure winding R and L, verify step angle, measure holding and detent torque.
      3. Load the motor and sweep step rate, recording torque, RPM, phase currents, input/output power, efficiency, pull-out, and missed steps.
      4. Plot results per the p.38 Excel method (scatter, smooth line).

      Motor type and theory (sourced):

      • Fundamental step angle θS = 360° / (2 n ZR) — Oriental Motor Technical Manual §3.4.3 eq. (3.2).
      • Holding / θ–T: T = −TH sin(ZR θm) — OM §4.1 eq. (4.1).
      • Resonance fres ≈ (1/2π)·√(TH ZR / J) — OM §4.2.1 eq. (4.7).
      • Pull-out / pull-in / start-stop / slew regions — OM §4.3 and Oriental Motor “Speed Torque Curves” article.
      • Constant-voltage vs constant-current (chopper) drive; Z = √(R²+(2πf L)²) — OM §5.3; TI SLVA321A decay modes; ADI Trinamic AN-026 microstepping.

      Sources: Oriental Motor Technical Manual Stepper Motor Edition (PDF on Oriental Motor EU); TI SLVA321A; ADI Trinamic AN-026 / AN-003. Book citation pending (owned Drive textbooks — book_sources.json not yet available at build time).

      Equipment:

      1. Hybrid or PM stepper under test
      2. Chopper (constant-current) driver with STEP/DIR
      3. Function generator or motion controller
      4. DMMs; optional LCR meter
      5. Prony brake / dynamometer / hanging mass on pulley
      6. Photo tachometer or step-count timing

      Safety:

      1. De-energize before rewiring. Stepper drivers can produce high bus voltage.
      2. Do not disconnect motor leads under current (inductive kick).
      3. Guard rotating loads; clamp Prony arm.

      Procedure (mirrors DC load labs):

      1. Measure phase R and L (or use Lab 8). Record rated V/I from nameplate if present.
      2. Verify step angle: command N steps and measure shaft angle / steps per revolution.
      3. Holding torque at rated current; detent torque at I=0.
      4. Couple a load. For each step rate in a sweep, record V, I per phase, torque, RPM, note missed steps. Identify pull-out.
      5. Compute P_in, P_out, efficiency. Leave blank any quantity you did not measure — do not invent.

      Discussion:

      1. Where did pull-out occur, and how does it compare with the theoretical curve in Motor Theory §7?
      2. Did you observe resonance? Compare with fres from OM (4.7).
      3. How did microstepping change vibration and pull-out?

      Graph instructions (p.38 Excel method):

      • Column A: step rate (pps) or RPM. Columns B+: torque, P_out, efficiency.
      • Insert → Scatter → smooth line; axis titles; chart title; fixed major units on X if current-like.

      CRITICAL: There is no measured stepper data in the 2012 manual. Tables below are blank editable fields. Graphs stay empty until you type values. Entries stay in localStorage on this browser; use CSV export.

      Lab - 8

      Winding Resistance and Inductance

      Objective

      1. Measure every winding resistance on a motor with the 4-wire voltage-drop method and with a DMM, then correct the values to 25 °C.

      2. Measure winding inductance with an LCR meter and calculate the electrical time constant.

      Equipment

      1. Variable DC power supply with current limit (Jon's bench supply)

      2. Two DMMs: one as an ammeter, one as a voltmeter

      3. LCR meter (with 120 Hz and 1 kHz test frequencies)

      4. Thermometer for ambient/winding temperature (DMM thermocouple, or (add) a thermocouple)

      5. DM-100A DC machine, IM-100 3-phase motor, and any PM DC, BLDC or stepper motor under test

      Safety

    • De-energize the console and remove all supply leads before connecting the LCR meter. Never connect an LCR meter or DMM ohm range to a live circuit.
    • Field windings are highly inductive. Lower the supply to 0 V before opening the circuit, or the field will produce an inductive kick. Never break a field current while it is flowing.
    • Limit the test current to under 10% of rated current (IEEE 113 practice) so the winding does not heat during the reading.

      • Procedure

      1. Record the ambient temperature t_a in Table 1. Let the machine sit unpowered for at least 1 hour so the windings are at ambient.

      2. Block the rotor so it cannot turn.

      3. Armature, 4-wire method: connect the supply in series with the DMM ammeter to the armature terminals A1–A2. Connect the second DMM, as a voltmeter, directly on the terminals and not on the supply leads. Set the current limit to 0.35 A (10% of the 3.5 A DM-100A rating, p8). Record V and I.

      4. Rotate the shaft about 1/3 turn by hand and repeat Step 3. Take three positions in total, because brush contact changes with position.

      5. Repeat Step 3 on the series field (S1–S2) and the shunt field (F1–F2), using the shunt field at 0.05 A.

      6. Measure each winding again with the DMM ohm range and record those values next to the 4-wire values.

      7. Induction motor: measure the three line-to-line resistances (T1–T2, T2–T3, T3–T1) by the 4-wire method.

      8. PM DC, BLDC and stepper: measure terminal R (PM DC), each line-line pair (BLDC), or each phase (stepper: A–Ā, B–B̄) by the 4-wire method. For the stepper, use rated phase current if it is known, and keep the test brief.

      9. Inductance: disconnect the supply. Connect the LCR meter to each winding. Record L at 1 kHz for the armature, BLDC line-line and stepper phases, and at 120 Hz for the shunt and series fields. Record the rotor position, and repeat at three positions for the armature.

      Table 1: Cold winding resistance

      (ambient t_a = ____ °C)
      WindingRotor pos.V (V)I (A)R = V/I (Ω)DMM Ω (Ω)R₂₅ (Ω, calc.)
      Armature A1–A21, 2, 3
      Series field S1–S2–
      Shunt field F1–F2–
      IM-100 T1–T2 / T2–T3 / T3–T1–
      Motor under test (each pair or phase)–

      Table 2: Inductance

      WindingTest freq. (Hz)Rotor pos.L (mH)R₂₅ from Table 1 (Ω)τe = L/R (ms, calc.)

      Parameters produced and derivations

    • R = V/I.
    • R₂₅ = R_t·(234.5 + 25)/(234.5 + t_a), using k1 = 234.5 for copper (IEEE 112, Purdue PDF).
    • Induction motor: R_phase = R_LL/2 for a wye connection.
    • τe = L/R (PHYS).
    • These fill the Terminal resistance and Terminal inductance rows of the maxon, Bodine and Baldor data blocks.
    • The stepper phase R and L rows match the Oriental PKP, Applied Motion HT23 and Minebea sheets.
    • Rated phase voltage V_ph = I_ph·R_ph (PKP/HT23 list voltage alongside current and R).

      • Discussion

      1. Compare the 4-wire armature R with the DMM reading, and with Lab 4's handwritten R_A. Leave Lab 4 as recorded. Why do brush contact and test current change the result?

      2. Why does the series field have much lower resistance than the shunt field?

      3. Compare your L at 120 Hz and at 1 kHz, and explain the difference.

      Graphs:

      none. These are tabulated values.

      Lab - 9

      Back-EMF Constant, Speed Constant and Torque Constant

      Objective

      1. Measure the open-circuit back-EMF against speed and find K_e and k_n.

      2. Show that K_t = K_e in SI units and cross-check against the load data in Lab 5.

      3. For a BLDC motor, capture the line-line back-EMF and the Hall sequence, and count the pole pairs.

      Equipment

      1. SPM-100A single-phase motor as the prime mover (as in Lab 3), belted or coupled to the DM-100A. Alternatively, use a second DC motor on a variable supply as the drive.

      2. DM-100A DC machine, plus the PM DC or BLDC motor under test

      3. Variable DC supply for the separately excited shunt field (0.5 A @ 125 V rating, p8)

      4. Photo tachometer

      5. Oscilloscope with two or more channels; DMM

      6. (add) Shaft coupler or belt for the small motor under test

      7. (add, BLDC) 5 V supply for the Hall sensors, with pull-up resistors if the outputs are open-collector

      Safety

    • Keep fingers, ties and leads away from the couplings and belts. Guard the rotating shafts.
    • Never open the shunt-field circuit of a running motor (runaway). In this lab the DM-100A is driven as a generator.
    • The scope ground is earth-referenced. Measure line-line voltages with two channels in A−B math mode or with a differential probe; never clip the scope ground to a live terminal.

      • Procedure

      1. Wound-field DC: separately excite the shunt field and set I_F to the value used in Lab 5. Record I_F and hold it constant for the whole test.

      2. Leave the armature open-circuit, with only the voltmeter or scope connected.

      3. Drive the shaft and set five or more speeds between about 600 and 1800 RPM. At each speed record the RPM and V_oc in Table 1.

      4. Reverse the drive direction once and confirm that the polarity reverses.

      5. PM DC motor: repeat Steps 2–3 (there is no field to set).

      6. BLDC motor: drive the shaft at a steady speed. On the scope, capture the line-line voltages V_AB, V_BC and V_CA together with the three Hall outputs. Record the peak V_LL, the electrical frequency f_e, the shaft RPM and the Hall state order in Table 2.

      Table 1: Open-circuit voltage vs speed

      (I_F = ____ A held constant)
      Speed (RPM)ω = 2π·RPM/60 (rad/s, calc.)V_oc (V)

      Table 2: BLDC back-EMF

      RPMf_e (Hz)V_LL,pk (V)Pole pairs p = f_e·60/RPM (calc.)Hall sequence

      Parameters produced and derivations

    • K_e = slope of V_oc against ω (V·s/rad). For the wound-field machine, K_e applies at the I_F recorded.
    • k_n = 1/K_e, converted to rpm/V.
    • K_t = K_e in N·m/A (SI identity, PHYS). The maxon and FAULHABER blocks list both k_M and k_n.
    • BLDC: K_e,LL = V_LL,pk/ω, stating the peak line-line convention; p = f_e/(RPM/60).
    • Cross-check, as a new column only: K_t ≈ ΔT/ΔI_A from Jon's Lab 5 tables (p29/p30), with torque in in-oz × 0.00706 = N·m.

      • Discussion

      1. Is V_oc linear with speed? What does the intercept represent?

      2. Compare K_t from this lab with the slope from Lab 5. Give reasons for any difference, such as armature reaction or field heating.

      3. Why must I_F be held constant for a wound-field K_e?

      Graphs (p38 method):

    • V_oc (Column B) vs speed in RPM (Column A), with a linear trendline that displays the equation.
    • BLDC: paste a scope screenshot.

      Lab - 10

      No-Load, Locked-Rotor and Stall Characteristics

      Objective

      1. Measure the no-load speed and current at nameplate voltage, and calculate the friction torque and rotational loss.

      2. Use a reduced-voltage locked-rotor test to find the stall current and stall torque of a DC motor.

      3. Perform the IEEE 112 no-load and locked-rotor tests on the 3-phase induction motor, and find the locked-rotor current and torque, the code letter, the breakdown torque and the equivalent circuit.

      Equipment

      1. Variable DC supply (0–125 V, HMD panel) and the 3-phase supply. (add) A 3-phase variable-voltage source (variac) for the locked-rotor test on the IM-100.

      2. DM-100A, IM-100, PB-100 Prony brake

      3. Two wattmeters (as in Lab 6), DC and AC ammeters and voltmeters, DMMs

      4. Photo tachometer

      Safety

    • A locked rotor draws high current with no cooling airflow. Raise the voltage from zero only until rated current flows, take the readings within 10 s, then return to zero.
    • Clamp the Prony arm mechanically. Do not hold it by hand.
    • Do not exceed the PB-100 limits: 432 in-oz and 3000 RPM (p11).

      • Procedure

      1. DC no-load: with the field at rated value and the belt loose, raise the armature voltage to 125 V (nameplate, p8). Record V_A, I_A (= I_0), I_F and n_0 in Table 1.

      2. DC locked-rotor: clamp the Prony brake so the shaft cannot turn. Starting from 0 V, raise V_A until I_A equals the rated 3.5 A. Record V_A, I_A, and the scale force F (oz). Return to 0 V.

      3. Repeat Step 2 at 50% and 75% of rated current.

      4. Induction no-load: run the IM-100 at rated voltage with no load. Record V_L, I_L, W1, W2 and RPM in Table 2.

      5. Induction locked-rotor: set the supply to 0 V and clamp the shaft. Raise the voltage until rated current flows. Record V_L, I_L, W1, W2 and F, then return to 0 V. IEEE 112 Method 1 uses no more than 25% of rated frequency. With a 60 Hz-only supply, note that the test was done at rated frequency (IEEE 112 Method 4, reduced voltage at rated frequency).

      6. Breakdown torque: run the Lab 6 load sweep at rated voltage and continue past the Lab 6 maximum in small steps until the speed collapses or the Prony brake reaches 432 in-oz. Record the maximum torque. If the brake limit is reached first, record "T_BD > 432 in-oz".

      Table 1: DC no-load and locked rotor

      ConditionV_A (V)I_A (A)I_F (A)Speed (RPM)F (oz)T = 6″·F (in-oz)

      Table 2: Induction no-load and locked rotor

      ConditionV_L (V)I_L (A)W1 (W)W2 (W)W_T (W)PF (calc.)Speed (RPM)T (in-oz)

      Parameters produced and derivations

    • DC:
    • P_rot = V·I_0 − I_0²R
    • M_R = K_t·I_0 (FAULHABER and Portescap list friction torque or no-load current)
    • I_stall = U_N/R, using R from Lab 8 corrected to the operating temperature
    • M_H = K_t·I_stall (maxon stall-torque definition), cross-checked by measurement: at the reduced locked-rotor current, measured T/I should equal K_t
    • Δn/ΔM = n_0/M_H
    • Induction:
    • I_LR = I_test·(V_N/V_test)
    • T_LR = T_test·(V_N/V_test)²
    • kVA/HP = √3·V_N·I_LR/(1000·HP), then the letter from the NEMA MG-1 10.37 table (the code letter appears in the MG-1 10.40 nameplate list)
    • R1, R2, X1, X2 and Xm from the no-load and impedance tests per IEEE 112 §5.9
    • PF = W_T/(√3·V_L·I_L), from manual p33

      • Discussion

      1. Why is the stall torque calculated instead of measured at full voltage?

      2. Compare the friction torque from I_0 with the T = 0 rows in Jon's Lab 5. Use them as recorded.

      3. Which kVA code letter results? Is it plausible for a ⅓ HP motor?

      Graphs (p38 method):

      DC locked-rotor torque (B) vs I_A (A), with a linear trendline whose slope is K_t.

      Lab - 11

      Rotor Inertia and Time Constants

      Objective

      1. Find the rotor inertia J with a coast-down (retardation) test.

      2. Measure the mechanical time constant τm from a voltage-step response and the electrical time constant τe from a locked-rotor current step.

      Equipment

      1. Oscilloscope (single-shot capture), DMM

      2. DC power supply with an output switch, or the function generator as a trigger only (it cannot drive a motor directly)

      3. (add) 0.1 Ω, 5 W current-sense resistor

      4. DM-100A with separately excited field, or the PM DC motor under test; IM-100 for AC coast-down

      5. Photo tachometer

      Safety

    • Keep the field energized during coast-down. Never open a running motor's field.
    • Use a properly rated switch to open the armature supply.
    • Keep the scope ground on circuit common only.

      • Procedure

      1. Coast-down:

      1. Run the motor at no load at n_0 (from Lab 10), with the field held constant.

      2. Connect the scope across the armature terminals.

      3. Open the armature supply and capture the terminal voltage (now the back-EMF) as the motor coasts to rest.

      4. Export or read V(t) at about 10 points into Table 1.

      2. Mechanical time constant:

      1. With the shaft free, switch a reduced step voltage (about 30–50 V) onto the armature.

      2. Capture the speed on the scope. A PM tach-generator or a second machine coupled as a generator gives the speed signal, or read the armature current decay.

      3. Record the time to 63% of the final speed.

      3. Electrical time constant:

      1. Lock the rotor.

      2. Apply a low-voltage step (current under 10% of rated) through the 0.1 Ω shunt.

      3. Capture the current rise and record the time to 63% of the final value.

      4. AC: disconnect the IM-100 at no load and time the coast-down with the photo tachometer, reading the RPM every 2 s.

      Table 1: Coast-down

      t (s)V_emf (V)ω = V/K_e (rad/s, calc.)dω/dt (rad/s², calc.)

      Table 2: Step responses

      TestStep V (V)Final valuet₆₃ (ms)Theory (calc.)

      Parameters produced and derivations

    • J = −T_loss/(dω/dt), where T_loss = P_rot/ω from Lab 10. This is the retardation method, IEEE 113 (cited by name).
    • τm = t₆₃, compared with J·R/K_t², the maxon/FAULHABER τm relation.
    • τe = t₆₃, compared with L/R from Lab 8.
    • These fill the rotor inertia and mechanical time constant rows that appear on 13 and 5 of the 22 matrix sheets respectively.

      • Discussion

      1. Why is the deceleration fastest at high speed?

      2. Compare the measured τm with J·R/K_t².

      3. Why is τe much shorter than τm?

      Graphs (p38 method):

    • ω (B) vs t (A).
    • Speed-step response vs time.

      Lab - 12

      Temperature Rise, Thermal Resistance and Duty

      Objective

      1. Run a motor at constant load until it reaches thermal equilibrium.

      2. Find the winding temperature rise by the resistance method, the thermal resistance and the thermal time constant.

      3. Confirm that the rated (continuous) torque stays within the insulation class limit.

      Equipment

      1. DM-100A with PB-100 (or the motor under test), DC supply

      2. DMMs, used 4-wire as in Lab 8

      3. (add) Thermocouple taped to the housing (DMM thermocouple input), and an IR thermometer

      4. Stopwatch

      Safety

    • Housings can exceed 60 °C. Use gloves.
    • Stop the test if the housing passes about 90 °C or there is a hot-insulation smell. Class B is 130 °C total (p8 Class B, 40 °C ambient).
    • Watch the Prony belt heating.

      • Procedure

      1. Measure the cold armature resistance (Lab 8 method) and the ambient temperature.

      2. Load the motor to its rated current, 3.5 A (p8), at rated voltage.

      3. Every 5 minutes record the time, V_A, I_A, speed, F, the housing temperature and the ambient temperature in Table 1.

      4. Continue until the housing changes by less than 1 °C in 30 minutes, or for 90 minutes at most.

      5. Shut down. Within 30 s, lock the rotor and measure the hot armature R (4-wire). Record the R value and the time since shutdown.

      6. Steppers: energize two phases at rated current with the shaft stationary and repeat Steps 3–5 on the phase resistance.

      Table 1: Heat run

      t (min)V_A (V)I_A (A)RPMT (in-oz)T_housing (°C)T_amb (°C)

      Table 2: Results

      R_cold (Ω)t_cold (°C)R_hot (Ω)ΔT_winding (K, calc.)P_loss (W, calc.)R_th,total (K/W, calc.)R_th2 housing–amb (K/W, calc.)τ_w (min, calc.)

      Parameters produced and derivations

    • ΔT_w = (R_hot/R_cold)(234.5 + t_cold) − 234.5 − t_amb. This is the resistance method with copper k1 = 234.5 (IEEE 112).
    • P_loss = I²R_hot, plus P_rot from Lab 10.
    • R_th,total = ΔT_w/P_loss; R_th2 = (T_housing − T_amb)/P_loss; R_th1 = R_th,total − R_th2 (the maxon Rth1/Rth2 split).
    • τ_w = the time to 63% of the final housing rise.
    • Rated torque is the highest load whose steady rise stays within the class limit.
    • The stepper temperature-rise row appears in Minebea as "80 °C MAX".

      • Discussion

      1. Does the rise stay within the Class B limit at 40 °C ambient?

      2. Why does the resistance method give a higher temperature than the housing thermocouple?

      3. How would intermittent duty (IEC S2/S3) change the allowed torque?

      Graphs (p38 method):

      housing temperature (B) and winding ΔT (C, where available) vs time in minutes (A).

      Lab - 13

      Stepper Motor Characterization (beyond Lab 7)

      Deduped against Lab 7: do not repeat R/L, step-angle verification, holding/detent, or the basic pull-out sweep already in Lab 7. Use Lab 13 for accuracy, pull-in with inertia, fS, and resonance survey.

      Skip any step that Lab 7 already performs.

      Objective

      1. Measure the step angle and step accuracy, the holding and detent torque, and the rotor inertia.

      2. Measure the pull-out and pull-in torque against step rate, and the maximum starting frequency.

      Equipment

      1. Function generator (TTL square wave into the driver STEP input) and DC power supply

      2. (add) A bipolar stepper driver with STEP/DIR inputs and a settable current limit, and a test stepper (for example a NEMA 17 or NEMA 23 hybrid, 1.8°)

      3. Oscilloscope and DMM

      4. (add) A 6″ lever arm on a shaft hub, a spring scale in oz, a printed 360° degree wheel with a pointer, or (add) a quadrature encoder

      5. Small Prony-style friction brake or a calibrated lever for loading

      Safety

    • Set the driver current limit to the rated phase current before enabling it.
    • Never disconnect the motor leads while the driver is enabled. It can damage the driver.
    • Clamp the motor to the bench.

      • Procedure

      1. Step angle: with full stepping, send 200 pulses (or N pulses) from the function generator in burst mode. Read the shaft rotation on the degree wheel and record steps/rev.

      2. Step accuracy: step one full step at a time for a full revolution with no load. Record the position at each step, or at least at every 10th step, from the wheel or encoder.

      3. Holding torque: energize two phases at rated current with no stepping. Hang the spring scale on the lever and pull slowly until the rotor slips. Record F_max. Repeat at three positions.

      4. Detent torque: disable the driver (windings open) and repeat Step 3.

      5. Rotor inertia: at rated current, give a single step. Capture the ringing on the scope, using one phase's back-EMF with the driver at standstill or the encoder output, and record the oscillation frequency f_n.

      6. Maximum starting frequency: with no load, set a fixed pulse rate and start abruptly. Find the highest rate at which the motor starts and stops with no lost steps. Check by stepping 200 pulses and confirming exactly one revolution.

      7. Pull-out curve: at each rate (for example 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 pps), start below f_s and ramp up to the rate. Increase the brake load until the motor stalls, and record T.

      8. Pull-in curve: at each rate, apply the load first and then start abruptly. Record the highest load that starts without lost steps.

      Table 1: Static

      Steps/revθs (°, calc.)Max step error (°)Accuracy (± %, calc.)F_hold (oz)T_H (oz-in)F_detent (oz)T_D (oz-in)f_n (Hz)J (kg·m², calc.)

      Table 2: Dynamic

      (driver current ____ A, supply ____ V)
      Step rate (pps)Speed (RPM, calc.)Pull-out T (oz-in)Pull-in T (oz-in)

      Max starting frequency f_s (no load) = ____ pps

      Parameters produced and derivations

    • θs = 360/steps.
    • Accuracy = max|error|/θs × 100. Minebea specifies ±5%.
    • T_H and T_D = F·r. The PKP, HT23 and Minebea sheets list holding torque; Minebea lists detent torque.
    • RPM = pps·θs/6.
    • J = N_r·T_H/(2π f_n)², with N_r = 50 rotor teeth for 1.8°. This uses the linearized torque-angle model T = −T_H·sin(N_r·θ), a textbook result for which I found no URL. Mark J as an estimate.
    • Pull-in, pull-out and max-starting-frequency definitions follow the Oriental tech reference (search-index text; the page returned 403 to direct fetch). Pull-out curves appear on the PKP and HT23 sheets.
    • Phase R and L: Lab 8. Temperature rise: Lab 12. Insulation: Lab 15.

      • Discussion

      1. Why is pull-in torque lower than pull-out torque at the same rate?

      2. How does the supply voltage change the high-speed pull-out torque? Relate your answer to τe = L/R.

      3. Is your measured detent torque a small fraction of the holding torque?

      Graphs (p38 method):

      pull-out (B) and pull-in (C) torque vs step rate (A) on one chart.

      ECET – 231
      Electrical Power and Machinery Laboratory

      Added 2026-11-04 — not in the original 2012 manual.

      Lab - 14

      Series Motor Characteristics and Generator Efficiency

      Objective

      1. Measure the speed-torque-current characteristic of the DM-100A connected as a series motor (p39 shows the series connection; no existing table covers it).

      2. Measure the efficiency of the DC generator, and the load characteristic of the series and cumulative-compound generator.

      Equipment

      1. DM-100A, PB-100, DC supply 0–125 V, photo tachometer, DC meters

      2. For generator efficiency, a drive motor whose output torque is measured. Options:

    • (add) Hampden DYN-100A-DM dynamometer;
    • a drive DC motor whose output is known from Jon's Lab 5 curves at the same V, I_F and current (used as recorded).

      • 3. Resistive load unit (as in Lab 4)

      Safety

    • Never start or run a series motor without load. Its speed rises without limit.
    • Tension the Prony belt before applying voltage, and keep the speed under 3000 RPM (PB-100 limit, p11) and under the rated 1800 RPM wherever possible.
    • Start at reduced voltage.

      • Procedure

      1. Series motor:

      1. Connect the DM-100A as a series motor (p39).

      2. Preload the Prony brake to about 200 in-oz.

      3. Raise the voltage to 115 V. Record I_A, V_A, RPM and F.

      4. Reduce the load in 24 in-oz steps down to no less than about 72 in-oz while watching the speed. Stop if it exceeds 2500 RPM.

      2. Generator efficiency:

      1. Drive the DM-100A generator from the measured-torque source at 1800 RPM.

      2. For each Lab 4 load-switch setting, record T_in, RPM, V_A and I_L.

      3. Series generator: connect it per p39, drive it at 1800 RPM, and record V_A against I_L for 4–6 load steps.

      Table 1: Series motor

      T (in-oz)I_A (A)V_A (V)RPMP_out (W, calc.)P_in (W, calc.)η (%, calc.)

      Table 2: Generator efficiency

      Load switchesT_in (in-oz)RPMV_A (V)I_L (A)P_in mech (W, calc.)P_out (W, calc.)η (%, calc.)

      Parameters produced and derivations

    • T = 6″·F (p11).
    • P = T·ω, with T in in-oz × 0.00706 for N·m.
    • η = P_out/P_in.
    • Series-motor speed-torque curve; generator efficiency η = V_A·I_L/(T_in·ω).
    • The series generator characteristic corresponds to the 110 V, 2 A, 1800 RPM series-generator rating on p8.

      • Discussion

      1. Compare the series-motor speed-torque shape with the shunt and compound curves in Jon's Lab 5.

      2. Why does the series generator voltage rise with load?

      3. Where is the generator's efficiency maximum?

      Graphs (p38 method):

    • Series motor: RPM (B) and I_A (C) vs torque (A).
    • Generator: η (B) vs I_L (A).

      Lab - 15

      Nameplate, Insulation, Mechanical Inspection and Datasheet Compilation

      Objective

      1. Record every nameplate field required by NEMA MG-1 10.40 (AC), the EASA DC list, and IEC 60034-1.

      2. Measure the mass, dimensions and bearing play, and identify the leads.

      3. Optionally, measure insulation resistance.

      4. Compile a complete datasheet from Labs 1–15 using `datasheet_template_and_test_map.csv`.

      Equipment

      1. Camera, (add) calipers, (add) scale, (add) dial indicator

      2. DMM for lead identification (continuity and resistance)

      3. (add, optional) Megohmmeter at 500 V DC. A DMM cannot perform this test.

      Safety

    • Use the megohmmeter only on a de-energized, disconnected motor. Discharge the winding to the frame afterward.
    • Do not perform a hipot (dielectric strength) test outside a qualified lab. Record the manufacturer's value instead.

      • Procedure

      1. Photograph the nameplate.

      2. Fill Table 1 for the motor type:

    • AC (MG-1 10.40): type/frame, HP, time rating, max ambient, insulation class, rated-load RPM, Hz, phases, rated-load current, voltage, code letter, design letter, nominal efficiency, SF, thermal protection.
    • DC (EASA): armature V/A, field V/A, winding type, max safe RPM.
    • IEC: IP code, duty, thermal class, PF, IE class.

      • 3. Mark any field that is absent as "not on plate". Do not fill it from another motor.

      4. Record the mass, shaft diameter, shaft length, mounting dimensions and frame designation.

      5. Measure radial and axial shaft play with the dial indicator.

      6. Identify the stepper or BLDC leads by resistance (pairs with continuity form a phase).

      7. Optionally, measure insulation resistance from all windings tied together to the frame for 1 minute.

      8. Compile the datasheet. List each parameter with its value, unit, conditions and source lab/page. Copy Jon's handwritten values exactly as recorded.

      Table 1: Nameplate fields

      (Field | Value | Unit | Standard requiring it)

      Table 2: Mechanical and insulation

      Mass (kg)Shaft Ø (mm)Radial play (mm)Axial play (mm)R_ins (MΩ @ 500 V)Lead ID

      Parameters produced and derivations:

      all read-offs, with sources for the field lists from the Machine Design MG-1 10.40 article, the EASA table and the CTC-N IEC 60034-1 text. Minebea gives stepper insulation resistance as 100 MΩ min @ DC 500 V and dielectric strength as AC 500 V for 1 min.

      Discussion

      1. Which required fields were missing from the plate?

      2. Which parameters on your compiled datasheet came from a calculation, and which from direct measurement?

      Graphs:

      none. The compiled datasheet embeds the graphs from Labs 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.

## v2.3: EE magnetic-theory layer (2026-11-04, America/Chicago; entry written 18:21 CT)

**Location:** `[local-path-removed]` (see its `README.md` for merge points). This is a standalone layer. Nothing under `v2/` was edited, the v2.2 build was not touched, and nothing was uploaded to Drive.

### What was built
- **17 widgets.** Each has an opening question, sliders, "Try this", "What you should notice", a lab/datasheet tie-in, a "Theoretical model" label with the equation, and sources (owned book first).
  - W1 Faraday/Lenz/flux linkage
  - W2 Ampère/MMF/Biot–Savart
  - W16 Maxwell in MQS form
  - W3 Magnetic circuits (reluctance, gap dominance, fringing)
  - W4 B–H/saturation/magnetization curve, with Lab 3 p.23 overlaid
  - W5 Core loss (Steinmetz + two-term fit to M-19, laminations)
  - W6 Permanent magnets (demag curve, load line/Pc, temperature, knee)
  - W7 Lorentz force/torque/shear stress
  - W8 Winding factors (pitch, breadth, star of slots)
  - W9 Lap/wave windings and E = KΦω with K = PZ/(2πa)
  - W10 Carter coefficient and slot permeance
  - W11 Cogging (LCM, C_T, skew) and stepper detent
  - W12 Armature reaction
  - W13 Lab 5 decoder (p.29/p.30, R_a from p.27)
  - W14 Design from scratch (D²L, electric/magnetic loading, R_a, thermal, τ_m)
  - W15 2-D finite-difference magnetostatic solver (FEMM-style workflow)
  - W17 Two-direction datasheet workflow
- **Two directions on one schema** (`v2/datasheet_schema.json`, plus a `requirement` provenance kind):
  - ① Characterize: Jon's Lab 4/5 values (tagged `example_jon2012`, page-cited), user measurements, or imported v2.2 state.
  - ② Specify/Design: load profile, duty, V/I limits, ambient, envelope, mass and inertia match → required parameters (`requirement`/`computed`, formulas shown) → W14 sizing estimate.
  - Use (a): a market table against the 11-motor catalog from `param_matrix.csv`. Values are cited by URL, blanks stay blank, and candidates that meet the spec are highlighted green.
  - Use (b): a manufacturer handoff spec with user-typed tolerances, producing test/method mapped to the ECET 231 labs, the NEMA MG 1 / IEC 60034-1 basis, and CSV/JSON export plus a print view.
- **Hooks.** v2.2's `#ds-market` and `#ds-build` stubs are intercepted in the capture phase, so they now route into the workflow.
- **Owned books.** `book_sources.json` was present (18:06 CT). 63 owned-book facts (14 books) are merged as Tier 1 "Owned (Jon's library)", each with its printed page, PDF page, Drive path, fileId and link. They cover 15 of 17 topics; MQS and core loss have no owned page, so those slots are marked citation pending.

### Verification (qc_v23.py → ee_theory/qc_report_v23.md): 17 PASS, 2 WARN, 1 PENDING, 5 FLAG, 0 FAIL
- **Published worked examples reproduced:**
  - Kirtley ch2 C-core Φ = μ0AN I/(2g), error 1.5e-7.
  - Star-of-slots vs Kirtley ch5 kp·kb on 7 cases, error 1e-15.
  - Zhu & Howe 2000 Table I (p.408): all 12 (Qs, 2p) → N_c, C_T rows exact.
  - Datasheet identities (Kt = Ke SI, T_stall = Kt·V/R, τ_m = J·R/Kt²) on maxon, FAULHABER, Portescap, Pittman and Bodine: 16 identities, worst 1.43 %.
  - M-19 two-term loss fit within 4.2 % of the table.
- **WARN, model limits:** a straight-line demag model gives BHmax −7.2 % for N42 and −18.6 % for C8, because the ferrite curve is not linear.
- **PENDING:** a published Carter numeric example. The RWTH/teee PDFs failed to download, so only the exact-vs-approximation internal check was run.
- **Dimensional checks:** 22/22 widget formulas.
- **Slider extremes:** 220 compute cases plus 231 real UI slider events, 0 NaN/Infinity.
- **Headless Chrome 156 (CDP):** 0 console errors and 0 network requests, both on the standalone preview and on the fragment injected into a temp copy of the v2.2 HTML. The temp copy also had 0 id collisions and hooks verified.
- **Citations:** 48/48 web/manufacturer quotes found in the text actually read, with pages computed from it. Topic→ref integrity holds. 14 claims are explicitly "citation pending". The privileged PEG document is not cited.
- **Jon's data:** E0 confirms the ee_data columns are identical to `v2/graphs_data.py`.
- **Theory-vs-lab FLAGS** (reported only, data untouched):
  - E1: Lab 3 slopes 267/333/333/400/286/200 V/A, top/mid 0.60, consistent with saturation onset. The 4 V residual cannot be produced by a single-valued model.
  - E2: the decreasing branch has IF ≤ the increasing branch at 7/7 points (hysteresis direction).
  - E3: the Lab 5 torque slope of 0.537 N·m/A is about 10 % below KΦ (0.600→0.562).
  - E4: the KΦ drop (0.937) tracks the IF drop (0.939), so it is confounded with armature reaction.
  - E5: compound KΦ rises 0.600→0.824, speed regulation 53.8 % vs shunt 10.8 %.

### What worked
- A shared physics core (Node + browser) let the same functions drive the widgets and the Python QC through node calls.
- Pages come from quote positions computed at build time, so no page number was typed by hand.
- The capture-phase hook makes the merge order-independent.
- The schema reuse means both directions export identical CSV/JSON columns.

### What fell short
- No Carter numeric worked example was read.
- Fitzgerald/Chapman/Kirtley's book were not accessed. Owned-book snippets were verified by the librarian pass, not re-opened by this job.
- MQS and core loss have no owned-book page.
- FD solver results are not yet compared with FEMM.
- DM-100A geometry (Z, P, a, Φ) is not in the manual, so W9/W14 cannot separate Z from Φ.
- Cogging waveform amplitudes and the magnet knee shape are illustrative.
- The absolute temperatures for insulation classes are user-entered (NEMA MG 1 table not read).
- Envelope dimensions are not in the catalog, so they are not judged.
- One mistake was caught in-session: a text edit broke the JS. The test now fails loudly instead of reading a stale result.
- A Python bytecode cache `v2/__pycache__/graphs_data.cpython-313.pyc` (17:36 CT) may have been written by an import of graphs_data; bytecode writing is now disabled in build/QC. No source file under v2/ was changed.

### Backlog (prioritized)
1. Merge the fragment into the v2.3 build at `#motor-theory` → `#lab-to-datasheet`. Add the `requirement` kind to `datasheet_schema.json` and delete the v2.2 alert stubs.
2. Plug `qc_v23.run_all(result)` into `qc/run_qc.py` and keep the merged-copy test (V23-C4) as a regression test.
3. Find a published Carter worked example, ideally from an owned book (Krause App. B p.626 / Gieras §4.2.13 are already mapped), and turn V23-A7 into a numeric check.
4. Ask the librarian for owned-book pages on MQS and core loss (Steinmetz, laminations).
5. Build a FEMM model of one DM-100A pole pitch once Jon can measure the bore, gap, slot count and turns. Compare it with W15 and Lab 3's air-gap line.
6. Replace the illustrative magnet knee with digitized catalog curves (Arnold N42 at 20/80/120 °C, MMPA C8).
7. Read the NEMA MG 1 insulation-class/temperature-rise tables and cite them in W14 and the handoff.
8. Add catalog envelope dimensions so the envelope requirement can be judged.

### What worked
- Collision scan: 0 id collisions across v2.2 / v2.3 / v2.4, and 0 global collisions (v2.3 adds EED/EECore/EET, v2.4 adds CTD/CTCore/CT24).
- Integrated QC is `qc/qc_v23_integrated.py` → `qc/qc_report_v23_integrated.md`. It runs run_qc QC1–QC12 on the merged page, qc_v23.run_all and qc_v24 (185/185), plus merged-page headless Chrome. Result: 56 PASS, 5 WARN, 1 PENDING, 5 FLAG, 0 FAIL.

All 17 EE widgets, all 12 control sections, all 14 v2.2 theory cards and the Lab 7–15 tables mount. Slider extremes produce no NaN. The #ds-market and #ds-build clicks land on #wf-mkt and #wf-hand.
- Merged bibliography: owned books are listed first, deduped by fileId + printed page (113 citations → 93 unique book pages). Other sources follow, then the 20 citation-pending items, all kept.
### What fell short / fixed in this build
- CSS collision, fixed in the merged copy only: ee-theory's `@media print{ body *{visibility:hidden} …}` would have blanked the whole manual on print. It is now scoped to an opt-in `body.eet-printing` class.
- A latent v2.2 JS bug was fixed in the v2.3 copy only. The self-excited generator widget threw `ReferenceError: V is not defined` when R_f was above critical. The v2.2 smoke test missed it, and slider-extreme QC caught it. v2.2 on Drive still has this bug.
- Remaining WARNs are carried over: the QC3 arithmetic in Jon's tables (P14 P_calc vs V·I, P33 PF > 1, flagged only, values kept), QC6 OCC decreasing branch, QC10 3 dead or 403 links (RDF namespace URIs and an orientalmotor.eu link with a stray quote), and the V23 magnet BHmax straight-line model at −7% (N42) and −19% (C8).
- QC9 still reads the original schema, so `requirement` is verified by I7 instead. The file is about 7.7 MB, which is not yet optimized (G-UX5).

5. Owned-book pages for the 20 citation-pending claims (MQS, core loss, bandwidth-separation ratio, PI R–L cancellation, 1.5·Ts delay, stepper mid-band resonance, PWM ripple, and others).
6. Fix the QC10 link extraction (stray `&#x27`) and teach QC9 the v2.3 schema.
